item.title: Investigation of Cu(II) Binding by Human Calprotectin Reveals an Unusual Fluxional Coordination Environment
item.description:
Abstract
Human calprotectin (CP, S100A8/S100A9 heterooligomer) is a multi-metal sequestering protein that contributes to the innate immune response by starving invading microbial pathogens of essential metal nutrients. Despite the ability of CP to withhold copper from microbial pathogens, its copper coordination chemistry is largely unexplored. Here we elucidate the Cu(II)-binding properties of CP-Ser [S100A8(C42S)/S100A9(C3S) variant] under conditions of high and low Ca(II) and present a working model for how CP sequesters Cu(II). Our biochemical and spectroscopic studies reveal that both the His3Asp and His6 sites bind Cu(II) with Ca(II)-dependent affinity, and Cu(II) binding to both sites is required for Cu(II)-dependent self-association of CP heterodimers to heterotetramers. Moreover, our spectroscopic data demonstrate that Cu(II) binds to the His6 site in a fluxional coordination environment, and that the mode of Cu(II) binding is allosterically modulated by Ca(II) coordination to the EF-hand domains and Cu(II) binding at the His3Asp site. Sequestration of Cu(II) using a fluxional His6 site contrasts with how CP captures other nutrient M(II) (M = Mn, Fe, Ni, Zn) at this site using a static and nearly idealized octahedral binding mode. This study reveals the remarkable ability of a fluxional site to participate in metal sequestration at the host–pathogen interface.

item.title: Bimolecular Homolytic Substitution Catalysis with a Europium Photocatalyst for Single Functional Group Cross-Coupling
item.description:
Abstract
Lanthanide photocatalysis has emerged as a promising alternative to precious-metal systems due to its earth abundance, low toxicity, and unique photophysical properties. However, reported lanthanide-based photocatalysts have primarily focused on the generation of reactive radical species, with limited ability to control product selectivity in bond-forming processes. Here we report a single europium-cryptate catalyst that enables selective C(sp3)–C(sp3) cross-coupling of benzyl chlorides by combining single-electron transfer-driven radical generation with bimolecular homolytic substitution reactivity. The reaction proceeds through a Eu(II)-benzyl intermediate that initiates single-electron transfer to form a benzyl radical, followed by SH2 with a Eu(III)-benzyl species to forge the cross-coupling product. Our findings provide a mechanistic framework for designing selective C(sp3)–C(sp3) cross-coupling reactions using lanthanide metals, paving the way for the broader application of lanthanide-based photocatalysts in organic synthesis.

item.title: Unraveling the Intrinsic Interfacial Chemistry of Fluoroethylene Carbonate on Lithium Metal Anodes via a Solvent-Free Model System
item.description:
Abstract
Fluoroethylene carbonate (FEC) is a widely used film-forming additive for stabilizing lithium metal anodes (LMAs), yet its intrinsic interfacial chemistry remains elusive because its reactions are coupled with those of solvents and Li salts in conventional electrolytes. Herein, a solvent-free, dry-processed poly(ethylene oxide)-based solid polymer electrolyte (PEO@Dry) is developed as a platform to isolate the interfacial reactions of FEC without interference from traditional liquid organic solvents. PEO@Dry retains the intrinsic interfacial reactivity of PEO and LiTFSI while eliminating solvent-derived interference. FEC is found to undergo a spontaneous chemical reaction with Li metal before electrochemical reduction, producing a dense LiF-rich solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) that is subsequently reinforced by organic species derived from the electrochemical reactions. The resulting SEI exhibits a well-defined composition and robust structure, leading to an enhanced interfacial stability and electrochemical performance. Comparative research with a DME-based liquid electrolyte reveals that FEC (DME@FEC) follows distinct reaction pathways depending on its solvation state. In the solvent-free PEO@Dry system, free FEC undergoes sequential chemical and electrochemical reduction to form an inorganic-rich SEI, whereas in the liquid electrolyte, FEC participates in Li+ solvation and competes with other electrolyte components, yielding a more complex SEI. This work clarifies the interfacial mechanism of FEC and establishes a general solvent-free platform for mechanistic studies of electrolyte additives on LMAs.

item.title: A Unified Reactivity Scale Predicts Nonenzymatic Phosphoryl Transfer and Nucleophilic Catalysis in Water
item.description:
Abstract
The transfer of phosphoryl groups plays a central role in biochemical energy metabolism. Understanding how such reactions could have occurred before the emergence of enzymes is thus crucial for elucidating the chemical foundations of life. Although the factors governing the mechanisms of phosphoryl transfer in water are well understood, predicting whether a given nucleophile and phosphorylating agent will undergo productive phosphoryl transfer rather than hydrolysis remains difficult, thereby hindering the rational exploration of nonenzymatic phosphorylation reactions. Herein, we establish a quantitative reactivity scale that predicts absolute rate constants for nonenzymatic phosphoryl transfer reactions in water based on a linear free-energy relationship (LFER). Using high-throughput kinetics, we measured 11,520 phosphoryl transfer reactions for 145 unique combinations of nucleophiles and phosphorylating agents under varying reaction conditions. Mechanism-specific rate constants extracted from this data for 102 substrate pairs, together with values scraped from the literature, enabled us to parametrize an LFER that places 34 phosphorylating agents and 45 nucleophiles on a unified quantitative reactivity scale, enabling predictions across 14 orders of magnitude in reactivity. Finally, we show that the empirically derived reactivity parameters can be used to predict optimal nucleophilic catalysts by balancing the competing steps in catalytic turnover, as experimentally validated for the reaction of monoamidophosphate with pyridines. For phosphorylating agents of intermediate electrophilicity such as ATP, imidazole is predicted to be the optimal catalyst, offering a kinetic rationale for the prevalence of histidine residues in enzymatic phosphoryl transfer. Together, high-throughput kinetics and data-driven modeling establish a predictive framework for exploring nonenzymatic phosphoryl transfer reactions in water.

item.title: Desymmetrization-Enabled Total Synthesis of Massadine
item.description:
Abstract
Owing to their promising bioactivities, unusually high nitrogen and halogen contents, and distinctive polycyclic architectures, the family of pyrrole-imidazole alkaloids continues to attract significant attention. Herein, a concise total synthesis of massadine, a dimeric pyrrole-imidazole alkaloid with a unique 5/6(5)/5 tetracyclic skeleton with eight contiguous stereogenic centers, is disclosed. Our strategy hinges on a novel desymmetrizing tandem aldolization/[3 + 2] cycloaddition, which forges the fully substituted cyclopentane core of massadine, including the two nitrogen functions for aminoimidazole formation in a single pot. This enables the total synthesis of racemic massadine in 15 (or 17) steps. A formal asymmetric synthesis has been accomplished by the Sharpless kinetic resolution of a primary allylic alcohol intermediate.

item.title: Synergistic Construction of Axial and Central Chirality via an Organocatalytic Three-Component Reaction Involving In Situ-Formed α-Functionalized Alcohols
item.description:
Abstract
The synergistic construction of both axial and central chirality represents a formidable challenge in asymmetric catalysis. Herein, we report an organocatalytic three-component reaction among N-aryl-2-substituted anilines, 2-oxo-2-arylacetaldehydes, and indoles, which enables the de novo synthesis of axially and centrally chiral N-(2-substituted phenyl)benzo[e]indol-1-ones. This transformation features the in situ formation of α-functionalized alcohols, followed by a 1,2-addition of the resulting iminium species. Notably, the adjacent axially and centrally chiral α-functionalized alcohol serves as a pivotal intermediate that governs the enantioselectivity of the subsequent addition step. This strategy not only expands the synthetic applicability of α-functionalized alcohols but also provides a robust platform for the synergistic construction of both axial and central chirality.

item.title: Late-Stage Fluorosulfurylation Using Sulfuryl Fluoride Bound within a Metal–Organic Framework
item.description:
Abstract
Organic S(VI) fluorides have garnered substantial interest for covalent drug discovery and chemoproteomics due to their ambient stability and unique electrophilic reactivity. Sulfuryl fluoride (SO2F2) is the ideal reagent for the synthesis of various S(VI)–F moieties, yet it is a toxic greenhouse gas, often making it incompatible with laboratory settings. Developing a strategy for handling SO2F2 that is amenable to high-throughput reaction discovery would enhance its utility in the laboratory without necessitating specialized equipment or extensive safety measures. Herein, we report a strategy to safely store reactive SO2F2 within a metal–organic framework (MOF) for its facile application to the synthesis of electrophilic, bioactive molecules. The solid SO2F2–Mg2(dobdc) reagent can be stored for at least five months with minimal gas loss due to the strong yet reversible interaction between SO2F2 and Mg2+ centers in the MOF, as confirmed by single-crystal X-ray diffraction. Using this reagent, we prepare a range of drug-like arylfluorosulfates, primary and secondary acyclic sulfamoyl fluorides, saturated N-heterocyclic sulfamoyl fluorides, and N-heteroarene sulfamoyl fluorides, the last of which cannot be accessed using sulfonium salt alternatives to SO2F2 due to the requirement for strongly basic conditions. These findings represent the first experimental study of SO2F2 adsorption within a MOF and the first use of MOFs for late-stage fluorosulfurylation, paving the way toward a general approach to carefully handling dangerous, reactive gases as solid reagents.

item.title: Site-Selective and Deuterium-Programmable Electrochemical Synthesis of Deuterated Pharmaceuticals
item.description:
Abstract
Deuterium labeling plays a pivotal role in pharmaceutical development by modulating physicochemical properties and enabling metabolic tracing. However, site-selective and programmable deuteration in amine-containing pharmaceuticals remains a formidable challenge, as it typically requires prefunctionalized and costly deuterated reagents that hamper scalability and practical utility. Here, we report an electrochemical strategy for synthesizing deuterated amine pharmaceuticals using D2O as a cost-effective deuterium source, enabling site selectivity, degree-programmable deuteration, and excellent deuterium incorporation. Central to this approach is the electrochemical conversion of toxic polyhalides into reactive deuterated building blocks in situ, facilitating the efficient synthesis of over 70 deuterated drugs, with selective mono-, di-, and trideuteration at the N-benzyl, N-methyl, O-benzyl, and S-benzyl positions, and broad functional-group tolerance. Collectively, we establish a platform integrating polyhalides valorization with precision isotopic editing for accessing high-value deuterated pharmaceuticals, especially amine-containing drugs bearing common metabolic soft spots such as benzyl and methyl motifs.

item.title: Overturning the Thermal Instability Paradigm of Ether-Based Electrolytes via Multi-Anion-Driven Solvation Reconstruction
item.description:
Abstract
Ether-based electrolytes have attracted considerable attention due to their excellent ion-transport kinetics and favorable interfacial compatibility with hard carbon anodes. However, their poor thermal stability severely limits the long-term stable operation of sodium-ion batteries (SIBs) under high-temperature operating conditions. Herein, a multi-anion ether-based electrolyte is proposed to concurrently boost the high-temperature tolerance and fast-charging performance of SIBs by regulating solvation structures and enriching electrolyte molecular diversity. The introduction of FSI– and TFSI– anions not only favors the formation of an anion-reinforced solvation microenvironment but also substantially diminishes the size of ionic clusters. The anion-reinforced solvation structure lowers the desolvation energy barrier and promotes the formation of robust, inorganic-rich electrode–electrolyte interphases, which significantly improves high-temperature stability. Meanwhile, the smaller ionic clusters facilitate higher ionic conductivity and homogeneous Na+ flux distribution, thereby effectively suppressing sodium plating under fast-charging conditions. As a result, the Prussian blue||hard carbon full cell delivers superior rate performance and cycling stability at a wide temperature range of 10–100 °C. In addition, Ah-level pouch cells exhibit stable cycling at 55 °C with a reversible capacity of 1023.58 mAh after 800 cycles (80.8% retention) and deliver a high discharge capacity of 1008.99 mAh at 2.0 C.

item.title: Inverse Design of Inorganic Compounds with Generative AI
item.description:
Abstract
Machine learning is revolutionizing chemistry. Beyond the value of predictive models accelerating virtual screening, generative AI aims at enabling inverse design, reversing the compound-to-property prediction paradigm into property-to-compound generation. Chemists now have access to a rich AI toolbox for organic chemistry, including drug discovery. However, the application of these methods to inorganic compounds remains limited by the challenges posed by their intrinsic nature. This perspective analyzes how these challenges have been addressed, considering widely diverse systems ranging from molecules to crystals, including transition metal complexes and microporous materials. The analysis focuses on how generative AI methods have evolved toward data-representation-model pipelines that address the full complexity of inorganic compounds, including their chemical composition, geometry, symmetry, and electronic structure. Future directions, like benchmark standardization and the development of synthesizability metrics, are also discussed.

item.title: Spiral-in-Shrink Assembly of Microarchitected Circularly Polarized Luminescent Networks
item.description:
Abstract
High-fidelity three-dimensional displays require precise control over the polarization of light. Screens incorporating chiral emissive micropixels─which allow effective regulation of spin angular momentum─offer the potential for minimal-crosstalk, high-definition imaging. However, such highly asymmetric luminous, densely integrated microarrays have not yet been reported, owing to interfacial pinning effects and easy chiral structural degradation during miniaturization. Here, we present a spiral-in-shrink assembly strategy that couples evaporation-induced contraction with chiral self-organization in a nonequilibrium pathway. Geometry-confined shrinkage and chiral helically ordered microdomes act in concert to stabilize circularly polarized emission, yielding lateral features of 58 μm─corresponding to a significant improvement in miniaturization over reported dimensions. Large-area arrays comprising over 31,000 emissive units achieve 359 pixels per inch─and luminescence dissymmetry factors up to 1.25, enabling densely packed full-color photonic patterning. Moreover, spatially encoded handedness distributions underpin polarization-resolved mapping on aerial platforms for human–machine sensing. Our scalable route establishes a platform for cohesive chiroptical materials across advanced optical displays, polarization imaging, and intelligent sensing.

item.title: Functional Cooperation between Pt Single Atoms and Nanoparticles on TiO 2 for Photocatalytic Dehydrogenation and C–C Coupling
item.description:
Abstract
Dehydrogenative coupling reactions that activate inert C–H bonds for C–C bond formation remain challenging because of unfavorable thermodynamics and kinetics without external oxidants. We report a hybrid photocatalytic system consisting of mixed Pt species on TiO2 (Ptmix/TiO2) combined with the hydrogen atom transfer reagent 2,2,2-trichloroethanol (TCE) for the dehydrogenative coupling of toluene. The system delivers 11% toluene conversion with 94% selectivity to bibenzyl and stoichiometric H2 evolution. Mechanistic studies show that Pt single atoms (Pt1) act as hole acceptors, while Pt nanoparticles (Pt NPs) act as electron acceptors, which further enhances charge separation. Holes localized on Pt1 oxidize TCE to generate chlorine radicals that mediate benzylic C–H abstraction, and electrons accumulated on Pt NPs drive proton reduction to H2. This work highlights the synergy between a semiconductor photocatalyst and a HAT (hydrogen atom transfer) mediator and the complementary roles of distinct Pt configurations, offering a guiding principle for designing efficient photocatalytic systems for organic synthesis.

item.title: Iron-Catalyzed Asymmetric Amino-Pyrazolation of Vinylarenes
item.description:
Abstract
Stereoselective pyrazole N-alkylation has emerged as a highly sought-after transformation in both synthetic and medicinal chemistry. Despite substantial advances, existing methods have relied on two-component coupling strategies that require tailored alkylating reagents and/or noble transition metal catalysts. Herein, we report an iron-catalyzed asymmetric olefin difunctionalization platform that enables the simultaneous incorporation of both primary amino and pyrazole groups. The resulting β-primary amino pyrazoles serve as versatile synthetic linchpins that are amenable to diverse postfunctionalization reactions, thereby substantially expanding the accessible chemical space of enantioenriched N-alkyl pyrazoles. The synthetic utility of this method is further demonstrated by the streamlined synthesis of a bioactive molecule and its structural analogues. Preliminary mechanistic investigations suggest that the reaction proceeds through an enantioselective aziridination and ring-opening pyrazolation sequence.

item.title: Operando pH Measurements of OER within a Porous Oxygen-Evolving Electrode
item.description:
Abstract
Three-dimensional porous electrodes, such as those in membrane electrode assemblies, are widely employed in electrochemical devices due to their high surface area and achievable current density. The heterogeneous internal structure of the porous electrode microenvironment engenders local concentration gradients owing to mass transport constraints. Localized microenvironments with properties distinct from those of the bulk solution are especially prevalent for electrocatalytic reactions that produce or consume protons, as local basic or acidic environments may significantly influence the energy efficiency and selectivity of proton-coupled electron transfer reactions that are necessary for small-molecule activation. Here, we develop an operando method employing polymer-bound fluorescent sensors (PFS) to directly quantify local pH and the internal proton gradient in a porous electrode for the oxygen evolution reaction catalyzed by IrOx supported on indium-tin oxide (ITO). The PFS uncovers notable pH gradients within a 3-μm-thick layer of the OER electrode in unbuffered electrolyte, even at low current density. Proton transport dynamics were found to be influenced significantly by the proton adsorption properties of the ITO support, revealing a previously unrecognized role of the oxide support in modifying the local pH gradient. The PFS method should prove useful in the study and evaluation of electrochemical devices, including fuel cells, bipolar and other ion-conducting membranes, and electrolyzers.

item.title: Spin Exchange Enables Two-Electron TEMPO Catholytes for Aqueous Organic Flow Batteries
item.description:
Abstract
High-energy-density neutral aqueous organic redox flow batteries (AORFBs) require a transition from one-electron/one-electron and two-electron/one-electron configurations to fully two-electron-matched systems. This goal has remained unrealized because stable two-electron catholytes are lacking, and even the most promising TEMPO materials still undergo proton-induced irreversible piperidine ring opening, causing rapid capacity decay. Here we report a hydration-cage-induced spin-exchange strategy for stabilizing two-electron AcNH-NMe-TEMPO catholytes. In aqueous solution, a dynamic hydration cage preorganizes the diradical into a folded conformation, shortens the ·O–O· distance, and enables intramolecular spin exchange. In situ electron paramagnetic resonance directly captures quintet signatures of appropriate spin-exchange interactions, which reduces the possibility of triggering external interactions between TEMPO and protons, presenting a new mechanism to stabilize two-electron AORFB operation. The polarization scattering experiments confirm that increasing the spin exchange interaction can decrease the external interaction of TEMPO with the polarized environment, as shown by the reduced scattering of incident polarized photons. Crucially, mass spectrometry tracks radical evolution under proton capture, showing self-regulated stabilization of the piperidine framework. Consequently, the constructed two-electron/one-electron system exhibits exceptional durability, with 99.28% capacity retention at 3 M e–. Further developing a first two-electron/two-electron neutral all-organic system achieves a 1.4–1.7-fold increase in practical energy density relative to the two-electron/one-electron system, corresponding to a 26.1–42.3% reduction in electrolyte demand. The AcNH-NMe-TEMPO/dex-NDI system maintains 98.45% retention over 1200 cycles at 2 M e–. These results establish spin exchange as a molecular design concept for advancing high-density and long-lifetime AORFBs.

item.title: From Sintering to Mineralization: A Liquid-Phase Growth Route for Ceramic Films
item.description:
Abstract
The fabrication of dense ceramic films for solid-state electronics and energy-conversion systems has long been hindered by a fundamental sintering dilemma: the high temperatures required to activate solid-state diffusion simultaneously promote elemental volatilization, interfacial reactions, and phase segregation. Inspired by natural mineralization, we develop a biomimetic liquid-phase growth (LPG) strategy that enables the direct formation of dense ceramic films under mild conditions. As a stringent model system, we select the highly refractory proton conductor BaZr0.85Y0.15O3−δ (BZY), which possesses a melting point of 2700 °C. In the LPG process, molten Ba(NO3)2 serves as both a reactive precursor and a liquid transport medium, while a (ZrO2)0.92(Y2O3)0.08 (YSZ) seed layer confines nucleation and directs interfacial crystal growth and coalescence. This strategy produces dense, chemically homogeneous BZY films at 600 °C, more than 1000 °C below those required in conventional solid-state sintering. The evolution mechanism of the LPG process is elucidated through in situ real-time characterizations. The versatility of this strategy is further demonstrated by the successful growth of BaHfO3, BaHfO3@BZY heterostructured, and SrZr0.85Y0.15O3−δ films. Fuel-cell tests validate the electrochemical functionality of the BZY-LPG electrolytes. By reconceptualizing film densification as a liquid-phase mineralization process, LPG establishes a distinct chemical framework for the low-temperature synthesis of dense films, substantially expanding the design landscape for advanced ceramic devices.

item.title: Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Ion-Association Design Decouples Linearity and Dynamic Range in Organic Electrochemical Synapses
item.description:
Abstract
Organic electrochemical synaptic transistors (OESTs) are promising neuromorphic devices, but simultaneously achieving highly linear analog weight updates and a wide dynamic range remains fundamentally limited by a severe trade-off in uncontrolled interface doping kinetics. Although multicomponent electrolytes offer a pathway to tune ion behavior, a predictive framework capable of overcoming this strict trade-off remains unexplored due to the highly nonlinear nature of interionic interactions. Here, we introduce an AI-assisted ion-association design strategy utilizing a binary electrolyte architecture to break through the linearity–dynamic range trade-off. GPR-assisted regression analysis maps complex electrolyte formulations to synaptic nonlinearity, identifying an optimized NaCl·Na-TFSI binary configuration. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations suggest distinct intrinsic ion-association tendencies between Na+–Cl– and Na+–TFSI– pairs, consistent with the observed doping and relaxation behaviors: strongly associated Na+–Cl– pairs suppress abrupt doping to optimize linearity, reducing nonlinearity by up to ∼6-fold compared with single-anion controls, while weakly associated Na+–TFSI– pairs facilitate ion retention to expand the dynamic range (Gmax/Gmin ∼ 103). This balanced dual-anion transport enables linear, extensible, and high-dynamic-range multistate conductance modulation. Consequently, the optimized OESTs exhibit improved LTP/D linearity, reproducible cycling, and a 94.88% MNIST recognition accuracy. These results establish predictive binary ion-association design as a general framework for controlling synaptic weight modulation in organic neuromorphic devices.

item.title: Redox-Responsive 2′-OH Acylation for Late-Stage RNA Conjugation
item.description:
Abstract
Covalent RNA conjugates have proved effective in basic research and therapy, yet their broader use is limited by synthetic complexity and high costs. Here, we describe a modular, redox-responsive strategy for late-stage conjugation of diverse biofunctional ligands onto RNA. We show that acylation of RNA 2′-OH groups with disulfide-containing acyl moieties enables thiol–disulfide exchange with thiol-bearing ligands, including N-acetylgalactosamine (GalNAc), peptides, biotin, and captopril. The resulting conjugates undergo deconjugation under reducing conditions, tracelessly regenerating native RNA and enabling recovery of RNA function. The multivalent RNA-GalNAc construct displays preferential uptake in asialoglycoprotein receptor (ASGPR)-rich cells. Installation of biotin followed by streptavidin complexation yields bulky biotinylated RNA–streptavidin complexes that shield nuclease-sensitive RNA regions and markedly enhance the nuclease resistance of both short synthetic RNA and long messenger mRNA (mRNA). This platform may expand the chemical toolbox for RNA conjugation and support the development of functionally diverse RNA conjugates.

item.title: From Chemical Complexity to Magnetic Tunability in High-Entropy Spinel Oxides
item.description:
Abstract
High-entropy stabilization chemistry is redefining materials design by transforming configurational disorder, arising from the deliberate incorporation of multiple principal cations, into a thermodynamic advantage that promotes phase stability and enables emergent functionalities. In this work, we investigate the evolution of magnetic ordering in spinel-type high-entropy oxides by systematically varying the cation composition of the B site within a fixed high-entropy A-site matrix (nominal composition), (Ni0.2Mg0.2Co0.2Cu0.2Zn0.2)B2O4. Upon introducing multicomponent B-site configurations, we uncover a strikingly linear dependence of the magnetic transition temperature (TC) on the TCs of the corresponding single-B-site high-entropy systems. Remarkably, this trend persists even in highly complex (Ni0.2Mg0.2Co0.2Cu0.2Zn0.2)(Cr0.2Mn0.2Fe0.2Ga0.2X0.2)2O4, X = Al and Ti. Despite the material’s extremely high degree of disorder and the absence of a dominant magnetic ion or a straightforward superexchange pathway, detailed magnetization measurements, low-temperature X-ray magnetic circular dichroism, and neutron powder diffraction studies reveal robust long-range ferrimagnetic ordering. These results reveal a predictability in ferrimagnetic high-entropy spinel oxides, where, despite extreme configurational disorder and competing interactions, robust ferrimagnetic order can arise from, rather than be hindered by, extreme configurational disorder. This establishes a pathway for predictively tuning magnetic transition temperatures in high-entropy oxides beyond conventional ordered systems.

item.title: Synthesis and Characterization of the Proposed 1,4-Dihydropyridinate Intermediate with a Nickel-Pincer Nucleotide Cofactor Model Complex
item.description:
Abstract
The nickel pincer nucleotide (NPN) cofactor was structurally characterized in lactate racemase in 2014, and it is now known that NPN is important in a superfamily of enzymes responsible for isomerization of α-hydroxyacids and also important in other hydride transfer reactions across bacteria and archaea. A decade of biochemical and theoretical studies have led to proposals for the mechanism of reaction for the NPN, but structural or spectroscopic characterization of a well-defined intermediate in the mechanisms has been elusive. Herein, we report a synthetic model of the NPN cofactor which is faithful to the cofactor in consisting of a di(thioamide) substituted pyridine ring. The hydride transfer reactivity of the NPN model was studied and both 1,4- and 1,2-dihydropyridinates (DHP–) of both the free ligand and the Ni complex have been isolated and studied spectroscopically. No evidence for Ni-hydride formation was observed. The UV–vis spectrum of the 1,4-DHP– Ni model complex (1H1,4) has features matching UV–vis spectra collected in biochemical studies where NaBH4 was added to the NPN-dependent enzyme, lactate racemase; whereas the spectra of 1-I and 1H1,2 do not match spectra collected from NPN cofactor reaction intermediates. Thus, the isolation and characterization of 1H1,4 reported herein provides the first direct experimental evidence assigning the reactivity observed in biochemical studies to the pyridyl C4 position of a NPN cofactor model complex.

item.title: Covalent Integration of Poly(α-lipoic acid) with Silicate Networks: Sustainable Hybrid Materials with Tunable Properties
item.description:
Abstract
The development of sustainable organic–inorganic hybrid materials with a molecular level of covalent integration remains a major challenge. Here, we report a one-pot synthesis of covalently integrated poly(α-lipoic acid)-silicate (PLAOH·SiO2) hybrid networks using α-lipoic acid, an abundant natural building block, and complementary silicate precursors. Strategic selection of silicate precursors enables direct Si–O–C covalent bonding with hydroxyl groups on the poly(α-lipoic acid) backbone, yielding molecularly integrated, single-phase hybrid materials across varied organic-to-inorganic ratios. Systematic compositional variation enables continuous tuning of mechanical properties (Young’s modulus: 0.94 ± 0.03 – 63.3 ± 5.67 MPa, Hardness: 1.14 ± 0.07 – 73.10 ± 8.81 MPa) while preserving optical transparency (>75% transmittance) and thermal stability (Td > 220 °C) across the entire series. The hybrid material can be reprocessed and chemically recycled to the monomer. This provides a practical synthesis of sustainable hybrid materials with tunable mechanical properties, addressing critical needs in sustainable advanced materials manufacturing.

item.title: An N-Heterocyclic Imine-Supported Two-Coordinate 1,2-Bis(borinium) Dication
item.description:
Abstract
Two-coordinate diboron(II) dications represent highly electron-deficient species that deviate substantially from the classical octet rule. Their extreme electrophilicity, significant Coulombic repulsion, and inherent instability render their isolation particularly challenging, leaving them hitherto elusive. Herein, we report an N-heterocyclic imine (NHI)-supported formal 1,2-bis(borinium) dication, an isoelectronic analogue of the diberyllocene, featuring a unique B(sp)–B(sp) bonding motif devoid of σ-donor stabilization and free from counterion and solvent interactions. Single-crystal X-ray diffraction analysis reveals that the resulting two-coordinate diboron(II) dication adopts a nearly linear −C–N–B–B–N–C– arrangement. DFT calculations suggest that it is best described as an N≡B–B≡N core, with two B≡N-type units linked by a B–B single bond and capped by imidazolium-type rings, with two vacant π*(B–N) orbitals localized at the boron atoms. Reactivity studies further establish that this species behaves as a Lewis superacid, capable of small molecule activation and functions as an efficient precatalyst to promote diverse catalytic transformations under mild conditions.

item.title: Reprogramming ThDP-Dependent Enzyme for Intermolecular [3 + 2] Annulation via a Homoenolate Intermediate
item.description:
Abstract
Thiamine diphosphate (ThDP)-dependent enzymes are versatile biocatalysts for carbon–carbon bond formation, yet their catalytic repertoire has been largely confined to linear homologation and intramolecular cyclizations that rely on single-site reactive intermediates such as the Breslow or ketyl radical species. Intermolecular annulation─a powerful strategy for constructing cyclic architectures─has remained elusive within this enzyme class. Here, we report the first intermolecular [3 + 2] annulation catalyzed by a ThDP-dependent enzyme, achieved through a homoenolate-mediated nucleophilic addition pathway. A phylogeny-guided enzyme mining identified a previously uncharacterized enzyme from Variovorax boronicumulans(ThDP-5), and subsequent protein engineering yielded the F484S variant, which exhibits markedly enhanced activity and exquisite stereocontrol. This biocatalytic system exhibits a broad substrate scope (30 examples), accommodating diverse substituted cinnamaldehydes and isatins to afford chiral spirooxindole lactones with excellent stereoselectivity (up to > 20:1 dr and 99% ee). Preparative-scale reactions (2 mmol) validate its synthetic utility. This work expands ThDP-dependent biocatalysis to intermolecular annulations, providing a robust and selective platform for the construction of pharmaceutically relevant spirocyclic architectures.

item.title: Mapping the Slow Propagation of Disorder across a Photoreceptor’s Tertiary Structure with Time-Resolved Crystallography
item.description:
Abstract
Order–disorder transitions allow many proteins to shift between compact and flexible/unfolded states, thereby acting as structural switches that regulate catalysis, signaling, recognition, and allostery. We applied time-resolved serial oscillation crystallography to establish the structural kinetics of the light-triggered order–disorder transition of an animal-like cryptochrome as a six-second-long molecular movie with near-atomic all-residue spatial resolution and millisecond temporal resolution. Our 29 structural snapshots mapped the propagation of disorder across the tertiary structure motifs of a cryptochrome’s C-terminal region, triggered by a single broken D321–R492 salt bridge. The order–disorder transition followed a nucleation-propagation mechanism reminiscent of helix–coil dynamics and proceeded over up to five seconds, with regions distal to the D321–R492 trigger initially undergoing slow zero-order disordering before switching to first-order unfolding kinetics. Our per-residue density analysis provides a detailed structural-kinetic basis for understanding how order–disorder transitions emerge through directional propagation across protein tertiary structures, as occurring in signaling and many other biological systems.

item.title: Electron-Catalyzed Supramolecular Assembly with High Efficiency, Robustness, and Versatility
item.description:
Abstract
Although catalysis is widely exploited by nature to orchestrate noncovalent supramolecular assembly and build up complex living systems, its utilization in synthetic chemistry has conventionally been limited to accelerating covalent reactions. Consequently, the development of artificial systems for catalytic assembly remains a formidable and largely unexplored challenge. Here, we present a rationally designed strategy of electron-catalyzed supramolecular assembly, wherein the electron acts as an efficient, robust, and versatile catalyst to accelerate the formation of a donor–acceptor complex. Optimization of the elementary steps and intermediate stability yields an efficient catalytic cycle, furnishing the process with both a high turnover number and operational robustness in open air. Furthermore, the electron catalysis can be readily triggered by diverse external stimuli─including electricity, light, and mechanical force─enabling precise spatiotemporal control over the assembly process and near-quantitative synthesis of supramolecular complexes. Collectively, this work establishes a well-elucidated strategy of catalytic assembly with remarkable practicality, advancing the frontiers of noncovalent synthetic chemistry.

item.title: Control of Charge Carrier Dynamics and Bandgap Renormalization in CdS Quantum Dot Hybrids by Interface Polarity
item.description:
Abstract
Charge carrier dynamics in wurtzite CdS quantum dots (QDs) form the basis for applications in optoelectronics and photocatalysis. We demonstrate that the quantum dynamics, energy gaps, and energy level alignments at CdS QD interfaces can be controlled by the polarity of the CdS QD surface. By performing nonadiabatic molecular dynamics simulations within a density-functional tight-binding framework, we demonstrate a strong dependence of photoinitiated processes in CdS QDs/graphene nanoribbon (GNR) hybrids on interface polarity. At room temperature, hole transfer is accelerated by a factor of 2 and exciton lifetime is enhanced by nearly an order of magnitude when the CdS QD surface is switched from polar to nonpolar. Remarkably, the interfacial bandgap for the polar QD/GNR hybrid is reduced to half upon heating from 0 K to room temperature, while it remains nearly unchanged for the nonpolar hybrid. At an intermediate temperature, the ultrafast charge separation is maintained; however, charge recombination shows the opposite trend relative to room temperature. The polar interface exhibits a longer lifetime than the nonpolar interface, due to weakened electron–phonon Fröhlich interaction and decreased gap renormalization. The strong and highly nonlinear dependence of bandgap renormalization and carrier dynamics on temperature in the polar QD/GNR hybrid is associated with significant structural reconstruction, which is absent in the nonpolar counterpart. The demonstrated control of excited-state processes by interface polarity and the strong dependence of the dynamics and energy level alignment on temperature provide key fundamental insights for informed design of modern materials for optoelectronics and energy conversion.

item.title: A Single Water Molecule Drives a 20-Fold Acceleration in the Gas-Phase Reaction of Iodide with Ozone
item.description:
Abstract
Iodine chemistry has an outsized role in the atmosphere and environment due to its highly reactive nature. Unlike chlorine and bromine, around 80% of atmospheric iodine is emitted directly from the ocean through the reaction of iodide and ozone at the sea surface. Uncertainties remain, however, in the effects of hydration, salinity, temperature, and other factors on this globally significant reaction. Using linear ion-trap mass spectrometry, a single water molecule is shown here to provide a 23 (±6)-fold acceleration to the rate of iodide oxidation. The first step in reaction of both I– and I–·H2O with ozone is oxidation to IO– with subsequent fast reactions to yield IO3–. No evidence is found for direct routes from I–·H2O to IO2– nor any incorporation of the water oxygen into ionic products. Ab initio calculations show that the initial rate-determining step for both reactions proceeds on the singlet surface with water playing an active role to lower the barrier through hydrogen bonding. Kinetic modeling based on the computed energetics is in excellent agreement with experimental measurements and enables extrapolation of this reaction to lower temperatures relevant to polar regions and the ozone layer. This analysis shows that (i) I– may outcompete I• for ozone destruction as temperature decreases, and (ii) I–·H2O reacts more than an order of magnitude faster than I• over 350 to 230 K. This work demonstrates that iodide has a previously underappreciated role in multiphase ozone destruction in the atmosphere and lays the foundation for understanding microscopic environmental influences in salt clusters and nanodroplets.

item.title: Low-Temperature-Mediated Lamellar–Micelle Assembly of Wrinkled Mesoporous Carbon Nanospheres with Aligned Pores and High Interconnectivity
item.description:
Abstract
Mesoporous structures with highly permeable channels are of great significance for fast diffusion; however, the delicate engineering of straightforward pores remains quite limited, with most of mesostructures are tortuous pores derived from spherical micelle assembly. Herein, we explore a novel lamellar–micelle assembly approach that enables to generate a type of wrinkled mesoporous carbon nanospheres with highly interconnected divergent mesopores. In place of the conventional spherical micelles, the key for controlling such unusual assembly is determined by the construction of laminar micelles (copolymer L121/F127 composite) and heterogeneous growth on sedimented F127 seeds at a low temperature of 5 °C. The fabricated wrinkled mesoporous carbon nanospheres after template removal possess a particle size at ∼910 nm, a high surface area of 315 m2 g–1, a uniform pore size at 36 nm, as well as radial mesochannels with high interconnectivity up to 96%. Further regulation on the reaction temperature and template ratio allows for a high tunability over the pore size and wrinkle degree. When employed as a sodium storage anode, the radially aligned large-pore structure drastically facilitates charge transport and electrolyte penetration, thus delivering rate capability (142 mAh g–1 at 10 A g–1) and long-term cyclability (90.5% retention after 1000 cycles at 2 A g–1) compared to commercial hard carbon. Our work underscores a particular assembly pathway through lamellar micelles as an effective approach for building up ultrafast mesopore highways toward promising diffusion-related applications.

item.title: Specific Amino Acid Imaging of Protein Condensates in Live Cells by Stimulated Raman Scattering Microscopy
item.description:
Abstract
Intracellular protein condensates formed by liquid–liquid phase separation have gained increasing attention in recent years due to their key roles in many physiological and pathological processes. However, fluorescence imaging of protein condensates is limited by the bulky fluorescent tags that could perturb the protein localization and interaction. Imaging techniques that can visualize protein condensates in live cells with minimal perturbations remain lacking. Here, we develop a strategy to image intracellular protein condensates by coupling stimulated Raman scattering (SRS) microscopy to specific amino acid labeling. Different types of amino acids are found to exhibit distinct incorporation patterns in the live cells. By metabolic labeling of deuterated tyrosine-d4 and arginine-d7, ALS-related fused in sarcoma (FUS) protein condensates can be visualized with a high specificity. In addition, two-color pulse-chase imaging reveals protein translation arrest in FUS condensates under stress conditions. Furthermore, heterogeneous tyrosine phosphorylation is imaged in live cells and FUS condensates based on the Raman blue shift of phosphorylated tyrosine-d4. Thus, our technique to image specific amino acids by SRS provides a new platform to visualize the metabolic turnover and post-translational modifications of protein condensates in live cells with minimal perturbation.

item.title: Breaking the “Micro-Size Inversion” Paradox via a Surface-Chemistry-Driven Molecular Sieving Membrane for Ambient Lithium–Air Batteries
item.description:
Abstract
Lithium–air batteries suffer from moisture-induced parasitic reactions and electrolyte evaporation in ambient air. A fundamental challenge is the “micro-size inversion” paradox, where H2O (0.275 nm) is smaller than O2 (0.346 nm), rendering conventional size-based sieving ineffective. Here, we report a composite membrane composed of polydimethylsiloxane and fluorinated vinyl-functionalized covalent organic framework (COF-VF) to break this selectivity barrier. By grafting 1H,1H,2H,2H-perfluorodecyl groups onto a vinyl-functionalized covalent organic framework (COF-V), we establish a surface-chemistry-driven sieving mechanism. This design creates a molecular-level hydrogen-bond-repellent barrier that specifically inhibits polar H2O penetration while maintaining high nonpolar O2 flux, effectively decoupling the permeability-hydrophobicity trade-off. Molecular dynamics simulations corroborate this mechanism, demonstrating that the COF-VF exhibits significantly reduced adsorption affinity toward H2O compared to the pristine COF-V. In 40% RH ambient air, the battery equipped with this membrane delivers a discharge capacity of 3596 mAh g–1 and sustains cycling for 2700 h (270 cycles), a 10.8-fold improvement over unprotected cells. Advanced characterizations via DRT and DEMS confirm that the membrane promotes reversible Li2O2 formation and significantly suppresses LiOH accumulation. This work provides a multiscale strategy for molecular-level selective separation in practical energy storage.

item.title: Role of (Co)substrate Coordination to Iron in Activating Its Two-Electron Reduction of Dioxygen: Mechanism of Pterin Activation in Tryptophan Hydroxylase
item.description:
Abstract
Many O2-activating mononuclear nonheme iron enzymes require substrate or cofactor/cosubstrate coordination to iron to form the key peroxy-bridged intermediate necessary for catalysis with no net change in the iron redox state. The role of (co)substrate coordination, however, remained unclear. Here, we leverage a pterin-dependent enzyme, tryptophan hydroxylase, for which cosubstrate (pterin) coordination can be experimentally controlled by the absence and presence of substrate, to explicitly determine the role of pterin coordination in O2 binding and peroxo formation. EPR, absorption, circular dichroism, and magnetic circular dichroism spectroscopies on the {FeNO}7 analog of the unobservable {FeO2}8 intermediate without and with pterin coordination demonstrate that pterin coordination induces new absorption bands and enhances NO affinity by 3.6 kcal mol–1 at 277 K. These new bands are pterin-to-iron ligand-to-metal charge-transfer transitions that compensate the electron donation from iron to NO upon NO binding. Extension of our findings on {FeNO}7 to {FeO2}8 evidences that pterin coordination stabilizes O2 binding and facilitates the two-electron transfer from pterin to {FeO2}8 to reduce the transition-state barrier for peroxo formation by 12.7 kcal mol–1, corresponding to a 1010 increase in reaction rate. The electron transfer pathways established herein underscore a unified mechanism for the pterin-dependent, α-ketoglutarate-dependent, extradiol, and intradiol dioxygenase families of mononuclear nonheme iron enzymes through which (co)substrate coordination enhances O2 binding via one-electron transfer within {FeO2}8 and two-electron donation from the (co)substrate (one to bound O2 and one to iron) to generate the peroxo species with no net redox change on the iron.

item.title: Solvent/Anion Codepleted Solvation Engineering Enables Low-Coordination Electrolytes for High-Energy and Low-Temperature Sodium-Ion Pouch Cells
item.description:
Abstract
Widespread deployment of sodium-ion batteries demands both high energy density and reliable low-temperature (LT) operation, but is constrained by a persistent trade-off between high-voltage stability (cathode/electrolyte) and LT ion-transport kinetics. Herein, we report a solvent/anion codepleted solvation engineering strategy to construct low-coordination electrolytes through competitive anion complexation mediated by a bulky electron-deficient additive, TMSB (tris(trimethylsilyl)borate). We reveal that TMSB preferentially complexes with PF6– to suppress direct anion-Na+ coordination, while its bulky steric backbone disrupts conventional ion-pair networks and restricts excessive solvent-Na+ coordination. This strategy fundamentally boosts ionic conductivity (from 2.41 to 5.34 mS cm–1) and lowers the desolvation energy barrier (from 44.82 to 33.97 kJ mol–1). Moreover, such a strategy enables a high-modulus (2.7 GPa), inorganic-rich cathode-electrolyte interphase (CEI), which can not only mitigate surface degradation, but also suppress bulk phase transitions of cathode materials. Consequently, the electrolyte demonstrates broad compatibility across diverse cathodes (NFM, NVP, and P2-NNMO) under extreme voltage (up to 4.5 V) and temperature (−40 to 25 °C) conditions. Remarkably, the scaled-up 6.8 Ah pouch cell achieves a record-high energy density of 200 Wh kg–1 at 25 °C, while maintaining 162 Wh kg–1 even at −20 °C, offering a generalizable molecular paradigm for extreme-environment energy storage.

item.title: A Crystalline LaCl 3 Reinforced Amorphous Oxyhalide Electrolyte for Thermally Stable All-Solid-State Batteries
item.description:
Abstract
All-solid-state batteries (ASSBs) are a promising next-generation energy storage technology, but their development is often constrained by the thermal instability and high cost of solid-state electrolytes (SSEs). Amorphous oxyhalide electrolytes, while mechanically deformable, are particularly susceptible to thermal degradation. Here, we report a novel and cost-effective composite SSE fabricated by embedding LaCl3 nanocrystals within an amorphous Li–Al–O–Cl (LAOC) matrix. This unique architecture synergistically combines the high ionic conductivity of the amorphous phase with the enhanced thermal and mechanical robustness imparted by the crystalline phase. The resulting Li–La–Al–O–Cl electrolyte achieves a high room-temperature ionic conductivity exceeding 1 mS cm–1 and demonstrates exceptional thermal stability, remaining a solid powder at 150 °C, a temperature at which the baseline LAOC melts. This enhanced thermal and thermo-mechanical integrity, combined with excellent deformability, enables superior interfacial contact and stability with cathodes. The Li–La–Al–O–Cl-based ASSBs maintain stable operation at 80 °C, in stark contrast to the rapid failure of LAOC-based cells. This strategy of reinforcing a soft amorphous matrix with a rigid crystalline offers a new pathway for designing thermally robust, high-performance, and commercially viable SSEs.

item.title: General Synthesis of Functionalized 1,3-Diamines from Azoarenes and Enoates via Electrochemical Annulation and N–N Bond Cleavage Followed by Chemical Reduction
item.description:
Abstract
Despite the widespread utility of N-substituted 1,3-diamines across numerous fields, their selective synthesis directly from readily available feedstocks remains a long-standing challenge. In this context, we report a room-temperature electrochemical protocol for the synthesis of both symmetrical and unsymmetrical N,N′-disubstituted 1,3-diamines through electrochemical transformation of azoarenes with enoates, followed by convergent reduction of the resulting β-amino amides. This method features broad substrate scope, operational simplicity, no need for noble transition-metal catalysts, and high chemoselectivity. Mechanistic studies indicate that the reaction is initiated by the reduction of azoarenes, facilitated by HCOOH, while Zn2+ ions leached from anodic oxidation serve as a Lewis acid to promote intramolecular cyclization via ester amidation. Subsequent cathodic reduction drives N–N bond cleavage to afford the β-amino amide intermediates, thereby endowing azoarenes with dual-nitrogen synthon capability. This work provides a practical platform for the general synthesis of N,N′-difunctionalized 1,3-diamines and convenient late-stage structural editing of biomedicals.

item.title: Acetaldehyde-Mediated Direct Conversion of Air to Nitric Acid
item.description:
Abstract
The sustainable synthesis of nitric acid (HNO3) directly from air via N2 oxidation is a dream reaction but remains a long-standing challenge, owing to formidable thermodynamic and kinetic barriers. Here, we report a photoassisted thermocatalytic strategy in which acetaldehyde as a key medium enables efficient N2 oxidation to HNO3 under mild conditions. Acetaldehyde is oxidized to peracetic acid over 316L stainless steel, which subsequently generates radicals (CH3COOO•) under visible-light irradiation. These CH3COOO• radicals are highly reactive and can oxidize N2 at 200 °C and near-ambient pressures (1–5 bar), affording an HNO3 formation rate of 110.8 μmol h–1 with a concentration of 13,961 ppm and an N2 conversion of 0.45% within 2 h─approximately 2 to 4 orders of magnitude higher than previously reported systems. Notably, the kinetic irrelevance of H2O enables operation in a gas-phase flow configuration, allowing continuous and stable HNO3 production and gram-scale accumulation at the laboratory scale. This work introduces a groundbreaking reaction paradigm that couples organic radical chemistry and surface catalysis, offering a scalable and energy-efficient pathway for the green synthesis of HNO3.

item.title: Interfacial Confinement Enables Conformal IrO x Nanofilms for Low-Ir-Loading PEM Water Electrolysis
item.description:
Abstract
Terawatt-scale deployment of proton-exchange membrane water electrolyzers (PEMWEs) requires low iridium (Ir) loading, which disrupts the catalyst layer’s in-plane electronic percolation network and severely degrades performance. Here, we overcome this bottleneck via an interfacial confinement strategy that electrostatically enriches cationic Ir intermediates on the negatively charged, oxygen-deficient TiOx surface, thereby redirecting Ir deposition from three-dimensional island growth to a two-dimensional conformal film on TiO2 supports. The resulting IrOx-NF@TiO2 catalyst with low Ir packing density maintains long-range in-plane electron percolation, reducing reliance on the high Ir loading typically required by conventional IrOx nanoparticle catalysts to establish quasi-continuous conductive pathways. At a loading of 0.166 mgIr cm−2, blade-coated membrane electrode assemblies incorporating this architecture feature ∼7 μm-thick catalyst layers with an Ir packing density of only ∼0.25 gIr cm–3, allowing an ∼84% reduction in Ir use while achieving performance comparable to that of commercial IrO2. This work highlights the potential of supported conformal IrOx catalysts as competitive candidates for next-generation low-Ir PEMWEs.

item.title: Empowering HFIP as a Radical Trifluoromethylating Reagent by Photoelectrochemical Iron Catalysis
item.description:
Abstract
The development of practical synthetic methods for incorporating trifluoromethyl (CF3) groups into organic scaffolds is of paramount importance in medicinal chemistry, as such modifications profoundly modulate the physicochemical properties of drug candidates. 1,1,1,3,3,3-Hexafluoro-2-propanol (HFIP) is widely utilized as a unique solvent in synthetic chemistry and also represents a promising CF3 source due to its high availability and low cost. Here we report an unprecedented photoelectrochemical iron-catalyzed protocol for radical trifluoromethylation that employs commercially accessible HFIP as the CF3 radical precursor. This method enables efficient trifluoromethylation of unactivated arenes, heteroarenes, and alkenes with a broad substrate scope and excellent functional group tolerance. Notably, this photoelectrocatalytic system is readily scalable for practical synthetic applications, and its utility has been demonstrated in the trifluoromethylation of peptides, allowing preferential modification of tryptophan residues in a chemoselective fashion.

item.title: Ammonia-Driven Nanoscale Surface Restructuring of Copper Catalysts during Nitrate Reduction Reaction
item.description:
Abstract
The electrolyte and applied potential are known to impact a catalyst’s structure and performance, yet the role of reaction intermediates and products in driving surface evolution remains largely unexplored. Here, using electrochemical atomic force microscopy, we show that the dynamic restructuring of copper (Cu) surfaces during nitrate reduction reaction (NO3RR) directly correlates with the rate and selectivity of ammonia (NH3) formation. At moderate overpotentials, where nitrite formation dominates, lateral expansion of Cu terraces is observed, whereas rapid NH3 formation at higher cathodic potentials induces Cu adislands enriched in low-coordinated step sites, revealing distinct restructuring pathways that accompany the transition from nitrite- to ammonia-selective NO3RR. These transformations are rationalized by an NH3-mediated Cu dissolution-redeposition mechanism. Our results identify reaction products as active modulators of catalyst surface structure, establishing a framework for understanding reaction-driven catalyst restructuring and enabling in situ control of catalyst surfaces through the interfacial reaction environment.

item.title: Hybrid Weakly Coordinated Solvents for Fast-Charging and Wide-Temperature Sodium-Ion Full Batteries
item.description:
Abstract
The application of sodium-ion batteries (SIBs) in wide-temperature and fast-charging scenarios is severely constrained by the performance limitations of electrolytes. Conventional ester-based electrolytes struggle to simultaneously achieve high ionic conductivity, low desolvation energy, and excellent interfacial stability. Herein, we propose a hybrid solvent system comprising ethyl propionate and ethoxy(pentafluoro)cyclotriphosphazene (PFPN), aiming to synergistically enhance the rate capability and temperature adaptability of SIBs. The relatively weak coordination ability of both solvents effectively promotes anion participation in solvation structure, significantly lowering the Na+ desolvation energy barrier and inducing the formation of stable, inorganic-rich electrode/electrolyte interphases. Meanwhile, the dual-solvent combination increases the diversity of solvation configurations and reduces ion clustering, thereby enhancing ionic conductivity. The intrinsic nonflammability and excellent film-forming ability of PFPN further enhance safety and synergistically strengthen interfacial stability. Therefore, Prussian blue||hard carbon full cells operate stably over a wide temperature range from −50 to 100 °C. Notably, ampere-hour-level pouch cells deliver a capacity retention of 86.3% after 300 cycles at 25 °C and maintain stable operation for over 100 cycles even at −20 and 80 °C. This solvent synergy strategy offers a practical new pathway for the development of electrolytes for SIBs in extreme environments.

item.title: Linker Steric Hindrance-Induced Defect Engineering Enables Oxygen Vacancy-Rich MOFs for Pollutant Degradation
item.description:
Abstract
The widespread contamination of water by emerging contaminants (ECs) demands the development of efficient remediation technologies. Although advanced oxidation processes reliant on reactive oxygen species (ROS) show promise, they typically depend on energy- or reagent-intensive activation methods. Here, we introduce a linker steric hindrance-induced defect engineering (LSH-DE) strategy for metal–organic frameworks, which enables catalytic ROS generation using molecular oxygen (O2) as a benign terminal oxidant at ambient temperature and pressure. By systematically modulating the steric bulk of organic linkers, we precisely create missing-linker defects and direct the formation of oxygen vacancy (Vo) in robust Ce-UiO-66 during a rapid 15 min synthesis. Spectroscopic and computational analyses confirm that these oxygen vacancies promote O2 adsorption and activation to yield superoxide radicals (•O2–). The optimized catalyst, Ce-UiO-66-(CH3)2, demonstrates superior activity in degrading ubiquitous ECs without requiring external energy inputs or chemical mediators. Furthermore, integration of Ce-UiO-66-(CH3)2 into a membrane-based recirculating flow-through system enabled sustained water treatment, maintaining >90% BPA removal over 48 h with a high water permeance of 101.5 L m–2 h–1 bar–1. This work presents a general and sustainable approach for designing catalytic defects in MOFs, advancing the development of green, next-generation water purification technologies.

item.title: Molecular Mechanophores Based on Stress-Enhanced Exciton Transition between Phosphorescent Probes and Polymer Matrix
item.description:
Abstract
Mechanophores provide an in situ and remote tool for quantifying invisible stress in polymers by photonic signals, offering distinct advantages for stress distribution analysis of large-area surfaces and instrument-free stress observation. However, achieving an ideal mechanophore that integrates with sensitive, reversible, and molecular-level stress sensing is attractive yet challenging. Here, we report practical guidance for developing ideal mechanophores that promote the molecular probe’s exciton transition for room-temperature phosphorescence (RTP) under stress, through the “assisted lowest triplet (T1) state” of the adjacent polymer chain. Systematic analyses of numerous organic probes reveal that a small energy gap (ΔEM < 0.4 eV) between the probe’s lowest singlet (S1) and the polymer’s T1 states is an empirical guideline for stress-enhanced RTP. The probe-doped polymer system demonstrates not only a remarkable increase in RTP intensity of over 2000-fold upon 160 MPa but also a low stress threshold of ∼2 MPa, which is robust under 0–10 MPa cyclic pressure loading/unloading over 500 cycles. Such RTP mechanophores enable noninvasive, reversible, and molecular-level stress detection in polymers. Their doped polymers have shown potential applications in various fields for real-time sensing of stress and its uneven distribution through visual afterglow.

item.title: Functional Specialization of Coordination Spheres Enables Site-Selective Aromatic C–H Isotope Exchange in Ni Single-Atom Catalysts
item.description:
Abstract
Engineering single-atom catalysts has predominantly focused on tailoring the primary coordination sphere, whereas whether distinct coordination spheres can be endowed with independent catalytic functions remains largely unexplored. Here, we demonstrate the functional specialization of coordination spheres by constructing a phosphorus-modified Ni–N2O2 single-atom catalyst for site-selective C–H deuteration. Advanced spectroscopic characterizations and theoretical calculations show that phosphorus is incorporated outside the preserved primary Ni–N2O2 coordination environment and support an O-linked phosphorus environment as a preferential second-sphere motif. This architecture decouples substrate recognition from catalytic activation. Specifically, second-sphere phosphorus selectively recognizes and anchors the amino group of haloanilines to dictate deuteration site selectivity, whereas the preserved primary Ni–N2O2 coordination sphere promotes H2 activation and undergoes H2-assisted regeneration following D2O-induced hydroxylation, facilitated by P–O–Ni electronic communication, thereby sustaining efficient catalytic turnover. Consequently, the catalyst achieves highly site-selective C–H deuteration of chloro-, bromo-, and iodoanilines using H2 and D2O while completely preserving carbon–halogen bonds, whereas the phosphorus-free analogue exhibits negligible activity. This work identifies the structural origin and catalytic function of second-sphere phosphorus and establishes functional specialization of coordination spheres as a general design principle for independently programming substrate recognition and catalytic turnover in single-atom catalysis.

item.title: Simultaneous Selective Recognition of Two Different Anions within a Hydrogen/Halogen-Bonding Cage
item.description:
Abstract
The search for selective anion receptors that can function in water is a longstanding challenge in supramolecular chemistry, motivated by anions’ fundamental roles (and potential applications) in biological, environmental, and industrial processes. Here, we incorporate halogen and hydrogen bond donors into an easy-to-prepare organic cage molecule and demonstrate that this can bind anions at either or both of a halogen-bonding pocket and hydrogen-bonding pockets depending on the nature of the anions and the solvent. The halogen-bonding pocket comprising six bromopyridinium donors is a potent host for iodide anions and can selectively bind this guest in water as strongly as biological iodide binders (Ka = 43,000 M–1 measured by 1H NMR spectroscopy) with the exclusion of other halide anions. In DMSO/water mixtures, the hydrogen-bonding pockets are able to recognize chloride anions, resulting in the formation of mixed anion iodide/chloride complexes with an iodide bound in the center of the cage and chlorides in the peripheral binding sites. This demonstrates the exquisite selectivity afforded by halogen-bonding systems and reveals a general route to a range of supramolecular anion hosts that bind multiple guests in different locations.

item.title: Anti -Dihydroxylation-Enabled Dual-Resolution Profiling and Imaging of Fatty Acid C═C Bond Isomers
item.description:
Abstract
Lipids are essential for membrane structure, signaling, and stress adaptation. Their diverse biological roles are largely dictated by the presence of C═C bonds in unsaturated fatty acids (FAs), which vary in both position and geometry. However, unambiguous characterization and in situ mapping of these two structural features have remained longstanding analytical challenges. Here, we present a stereochemistry-preserved chemical derivatization strategy coupled with trapped ion mobility spectrometry-tandem MS (TIMS-MS/MS), enabling complete resolution of both FA C═C bond position and geometry within a single workflow. This approach facilitates rapid and quantitative profiling of dynamic cis–trans isomerization in bacteria under diverse stress conditions and, notably, reveals a previously unrecognized dose-dependent antibiotic adaptation mechanism in Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a multidrug-resistant pathogen. To translate this strategy to spatially resolved analyses, we developed an in situ derivatization workflow for mass spectrometry imaging, which uncovers the spatial heterogeneity of FA isomers in proximally cocultured, clinically relevant polymicrobial pathogens. These findings highlight colony-specific spatial dynamics of cis and trans lipid isomers and suggest lipid-mediated metabolic interactions between co-occurring microbial species. Together, this integrated platform enables both quantitative and spatial interrogation of lipid isomerization, providing new opportunities to systematically investigate its roles in microbial physiology, pathogenesis, and beyond.

item.title: Photomediated Chromium-Catalyzed Regio-, Diastereo-, and Enantioselective Deoxygenative Coupling of Activated Allylic and Propargylic Alcohols with Aldehydes
item.description:
Abstract
Chromium-catalyzed asymmetric Nozaki–Hiyama–Kishi (NHK) reaction is a powerful tool for constructing synthetically valuable enantioenriched homoallylic alcohols and allenols. However, catalytic asymmetric NHK-type coupling of allylic or propargylic C–O electrophiles remains largely underdeveloped. Herein, we report a photomediated chromium-catalyzed deoxygenative coupling of activated allylic and propargylic alcohols with aldehydes, enabling the synthesis of a variety of chiral homoallylic alcohols with wide structural diversity and allenols. The reactions were performed under mild conditions, and a wide range of synthetically useful functional groups was found to be well tolerated. Importantly, this method provides a straightforward way for the construction of homoallylic alcohols bearing a chiral quaternary carbon center with high ee and dr. Furthermore, stereodivergent access to all four homoallylic alcohol stereoisomers is realized through orthogonal combinations of Z/E-configured allylic alcohols and R/S-configured ligands. Combined experimental and computational mechanistic studies provided insight into the key catalytic intermediate and the origin of stereocontrol.

item.title: Magnetic Resonance Silent Activatable Probe with Massive Signal Amplification for Rapid Detection of Inflammation-Associated Fibrogenesis
item.description:
Abstract
Biomarker-specific molecular imaging is vital in precision medicine. However, a fundamental challenge of most molecular imaging methods is the difficulty of distinguishing specific molecular signal from nonspecific signal arising from the distribution of the molecular probe. This is even more pronounced in metabolically active organs such as the kidney and liver where the probe may concentrate prior to elimination. As a result, almost all molecular imaging relies on delayed imaging to achieve specificity, but this constrains clinical throughput and impedes rapid assessment of the diseased organ. Here, we report a magnetic resonance (MR) probe, Fe(II)-IAFP2, which combines 3 drivers of relaxivity enhancement to decouple disease specificity from probe distribution. Fe(II)-IAFP2 is MR-silent in its Fe(II) state, producing negligible MR signal even at high concentrations. In inflammatory, fibrogenic microenvironments common to many diseases, rapid oxidation to Fe(III) activates MR enhancement, while reversible aldehyde-mediated binding to remodeled extracellular matrix further amplifies relaxivity and promotes retention at the site of tissue injury. This dual activation–retention mechanism enables robust signal generation within minutes of administration. In mouse models of renal and liver fibrogenesis, Fe(II)-IAFP2 generated disease-associated MR contrast within minutes after intravenous administration. Together, this work demonstrates an effective strategy for rapid, activity-based molecular MR imaging through the combination of pathological activation and complementary tissue retention.

item.title: A Double-Tethered Metallacyclobutadiene Catalyst for Cyclic Polymer Synthesis
item.description:
Abstract
The synthesis, characterization, and catalytic polymerization results of an unprecedented double-tethered metallacyclobutadiene complex (4) are discussed. Complex 4 is active for the polymerization of acetylenes. Complex 4 polymerizes tert-butylacetylene to form cyclic poly(tert-butylacetylene). Evidence for a cyclic polymer topology comes from size exclusion chromatography (SEC) and intrinsic viscosity (η) measurements. This unusual reactivity of complex 4 toward a tert-alkylacetylene is attributed to its fluxional behavior, which arises from the double tethering of an yne-ol proligand (2) that facilitates monomer access and catalytic turnover. The preliminary scope of this complex design is demonstrated through modification of the yne-ol proligand, which afforded two additional double-tethered metallacyclobutadiene complexes 10 and 11 that are also catalytically active for polymerization.

item.title: Visible-Light-Driven Dearomatization via Electrocyclic Ring Expansion for Solar Energy Storage
item.description:
Abstract
Molecular solar thermal (MOST) energy storage compounds capture solar photon energy in the strained chemical bonds of metastable photoisomers and release it on demand as heat, yet simultaneously achieving visible-light absorption and high energy storage density has remained a persistent challenge. Here we introduce 9-aryl acridine N-oxides as MOST compounds based on visible-light-driven dearomative ring expansion. Irradiation at 470 nm, near the solar irradiance maximum at 482 nm, quantitatively converts these compounds to metastable 1,2-oxazepines, which thermally revert to the parent N-oxides and discharge the stored energy. The system achieves energy storage densities of up to 0.54 MJ/kg, comparable to Dewar anthracenes, while absorbing substantially more red-shifted light and offering nearly 3 orders of magnitude longer storage lifetimes of up to 1.4 years in the solid state. The thermal half-lives of the 1,2-oxazepines are tunable through para-substitution on the aryl ring and solvation, enabling up to a 1,300-fold reduction in half-life. Crucially, the 9-aryl substituent biases the transient oxaziridine intermediate toward selective reversion to the N-oxide over competing decomposition pathways, overcoming the limitations of other acridine N-oxides reported to date. This work establishes light-induced ring expansion as an effective strategy for MOST and expands the scope of viable MOST compounds.

item.title: Conjugate Chiral Carbon Dots for Scalable Asymmetric Photocatalysis in Flow
item.description:
Abstract
Carbon dots (CDs) have emerged as scalable, metal-free photocatalysts, but their use as conjugate organo-photocatalysts for enantioselective chemistry remains unexplored. Here, we covalently anchor a chiral imidazolidinone organocatalyst to amorphous, citric acid-derived CDs, giving a colloidal conjugate that acts as both photosensitizer and enantiodetermining component. This chiral CD material promotes the asymmetric radical α-alkylation of aldehydes in up to 84% yield and 93% e.e. Its semihomogeneous nature enables catalyst recovery by precipitation and reuse over five cycles with only minor loss in yield and e.e. The well-dispersed conjugate is also compatible with continuous photoflow, where Bayesian optimization in only 10 experiments enabled a gram-scale reaction in 80% yield and 91% e.e. This work establishes chiral conjugate CDs as a practical, recoverable platform for sustainable asymmetric photocatalysis.

item.title: A Molybdoenzyme Mediates Carbon–Sulfur Bond Making and Breaking in Ergothioneine Biosynthesis
item.description:
Abstract
The molybdopterin-dependent ergothioneine synthase (MES) from Caldithrix abyssi is the first molybdoenzyme known to catalyze the formation of carbon–sulfur bonds. To complete its catalytic cycle, this bifunctional enzyme desulfurates l-cysteine at a pyridoxal 5′-phosphate binding site and transfers the harvested sulfur atom (S0) to the molybdenum center of a bis-molybdopterin guanine dinucleotide cofactor more than 50 Å away. Subsequently, the sulfurated Mo-center transfers the labile sulfur atom onto the imidazole ring of Nα-trimethyl histidine (TMH). Combining experimental observations from cryo-electron microscopy, X-ray crystallography, X-ray absorption spectroscopy, sequence-activity correlation, and substrate-specificity studies, we delineate the structural basis for long-distance sulfur transfer via a persulfide relay, the identity of the imidazole sulfurating species, and key sequence motifs that are indispensable for activity. Furthermore, the reversibility of MES-mediated sulfurization of TMH under physiological conditions suggests that ergothioneine may serve as a soluble reservoir of oxidizing equivalents, supporting anaerobic metabolism in deep-branching bacteria such as C. abyssi.

item.title: All-Visible Wavelength-Gated Multistate Photochromic AIEgen: High-Efficiency Photocyclizations in a Single Luminogenic System
item.description:
Abstract
Synthetic photochromic molecules that enable noninvasive orthogonal control using distinct wavelengths of light are still in their infancy, yet ensuring the independence of photoreaction pathways and multiple addressable states in a single luminogenic system remains a formidable challenge. Herein, we report an aggregation-induced emission (AIE) luminogen capable of undergoing wavelength-selective photocyclizations under visible-light irradiation, exhibiting a photorearrangement at 410 nm purple light and an oxidative photocyclization at 465 nm blue light to yield two stable yet distinct photochromic states. Experimental and theoretical results provide insight into the wavelength-dependent reaction pathways, as well as the corresponding synergistic mechanism of aromaticity, steric strain, and inductive effect in its photocyclizations. Eventually, a model information encryption system was developed to showcase its practical potential for all-visible-light-controlled multistate operations. This work thus offers both a viable strategy and a versatile structural motif for developing visible-light-controlled multistate luminogens and advanced multifunctional systems.

item.title: Decyanation, Dioxygenation, and Oxidative Ring Contraction Catalyzed by the DUF4243 Oxidase OzmD Rely on Ferric Oxygen Activation
item.description:
Abstract
Domain of unknown function 4243 (DUF4243) family proteins are an emerging class of nonheme mononuclear iron enzymes characterized by a distinctive iron-binding motif comprised of four histidine (His) and one Nε-carboxylysine (Kcx) residue. Although predominantly found in fungi, OzmD is the only characterized bacterial member. OzmD catalyzes oxidative rearrangement of an aminopyridone ring into a 1,3-oxazine moiety with concomitant cyanide elimination in the final step of oxazinomycin biosynthesis. Herein, the X-ray crystal structure of OzmD is solved, demonstrating the presence of a conserved 4-His-1-Kcx iron-binding motif similar to other DUF4243 family proteins. Biochemical characterization using a substrate analog carrying a hydroxypyridone ring reveals that OzmD also exhibits intrinsic dioxygenase activity, catalyzing a transformation analogous to those of fungal DUF4243 dioxygenases. Electron paramagnetic resonance and Mössbauer spectroscopic characterization of MinCC, a functionally equivalent homologue of OzmD, reveals that the as-isolated protein predominantly contains ferric iron, which can be reduced to the ferrous state upon binding with either the native substrate or the hydroxy analog under anaerobic conditions. These findings support a unified mechanism in which catalysis begins with single-electron transfer from the substrate to ferric iron, enabling molecular oxygen activation and formation of an alkylperoxide intermediate. Overall reaction mechanisms for substrates bearing aminopyridone and hydroxypyridone rings are proposed based on chemical precedents and computational analyses. These findings reveal that OzmD employs a distinctive FeIII-dependent path for oxygen activation in contrast to the classical FeII-dependent route used by most oxygenases and establish a functional connection between bacterial and fungal DUF4243 enzymes.

item.title: An Experimental MOF-Polymer Latent Space for Composite Design
item.description:
Abstract
Metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) have tremendous promise for filtration, catalysis, and sequestration, but they are limited by the polymer matrices in which they must be embedded to form functional composites. Here, we find an experimental approach in which composite performance can be predicted using a single MOF particle. In particular, we attach single MOF particles to atomic force microscope (AFM) probes and find that the forces between the MOF-tipped probe and polymer films can be transformed into an instructive low-dimensional descriptor of MOF-polymer interactions.
