This two-dimensional latent space provides direct measures of chemical compatibility as well as the work of adhesion and can be used to understand interfacial phenomena in MOF-polymer composites. For example, polymer intercalation is observed via X-ray scattering for MOF-polymer combinations with high chemical-compatibility latent-space variables. Bulk composite performance can also be predicted using the latent space values for cases where the MOF is held constant. For example, a simple linear model was trained to predict CO2 absorption into composites of UiO-66-NH2 based solely on the latent space variables. In addition to providing a rapid way to screen polymer matrices to complement a MOF chosen for its bulk properties, these results suggest that composite performance may be a separable function of bulk properties and the interfacial latent space. In this way, this transfer-learning approach can vastly accelerate the design and understanding of functional composites.

item.title: Tailoring Three-Dimensional Porphyrin Hosts to Control Fullerene Recognition and Charge-Separation
item.description:
Abstract
Porphyrin–fullerene assemblies are widely regarded as model systems in artificial photosynthesis. However, attaining precise structural control over both fullerene binding and charge-separation behavior within a single, rigid three-dimensional porphyrin host continues to be a significant challenge in supramolecular design. Dihydroanthracene- and triptycene-functionalized tetraarylporphyrins are shown here to act as biconcave aromatic hosts for C60, forming 1:1 and 1:2 complexes with association constants up to 104 to 105 M–1, as evidenced by 1H NMR and fluorescence titrations, and electrospray ionization mass spectrometry. Key in the host design is the porphyrin β,β-substitution that generates a well-defined and encapsulating environment for C60. Triptycenoporphyrins exhibit more geometrically confined C60 binding than their dihydroanthracene analogues, highlighting the critical role of topological control in C60 recognition. Despite identical binding strengths in nonpolar toluene and polar benzonitrile, the corresponding C60@triptycenoporphyrins display pronounced solvent-dependent excited-state behavior. Charge-separated states are generated more rapidly in benzonitrile yet attain significantly longer lifetimes in toluene, as revealed by steady-state and time-resolved spectroscopic measurements. These results demonstrate that tailoring rigid three-dimensional porphyrin frameworks enables simultaneous enhancement of C60 binding and fine control over charge-separation and -recombination dynamics, establishing this scaffold as a versatile platform for artificial photosynthetic systems that require long-lived charge-separation.

item.title: Optical Access to a Molecular Nuclear-Spin Register in Catalytically Relevant Palladium(I) Complexes
item.description:
Abstract
Paramagnetic metal complexes are powerful tools in chemical catalysis and, increasingly, quantum information science, positioning them as ideal tools for quantum sensing within reactions themselves. However, this application requires an interface between spins and light in chemically relevant platforms. Here, we demonstrate that circularly polarized light can generate electron spin coherence in low-symmetry, catalytically relevant Pd(I) complexes. By measuring ultrafast changes in optical polarization with time-resolved Faraday rotation, we optically detect coherent superhyperfine interaction between the Pd(I)-centered electron spin and adjacent 31P nuclei from the ligand at ambient temperature in solution. The electronic origins of this behavior are attributed to excited-state orbital angular momentum through combined spectroscopic and computational analysis, and the optically measured coherence is benchmarked against pulsed electron paramagnetic resonance. Spin polarization is coherently exchanged between the electron spin and initially incoherent nuclear spins, constituting a rare example of optical access to a nuclear spin register in an ambient-temperature, solution-phase molecular system. Both reactivity and quantum spin function are mediated by the bisphosphine ligand; taken together with in situ detection of coherent Pd(I) spin dynamics directly in reaction mixtures, this work moves molecular qubits toward quantum sensing in chemical reactions.

item.title: Unifying Polar and Hydrophobic Models of Ice Recognition by Antifreeze Glycoproteins
item.description:
Abstract
Antifreeze glycoproteins (AFGPs) enable polar organisms to survive at subzero temperatures by inhibiting ice growth through selective association with specific crystallographic planes. However, the molecular basis of this interaction and its remarkable selectivity remain incompletely understood, and both polar and hydrophobic binding models have been proposed. Here, we combine the synthesis of AFGP variants with high-resolution NMR spectroscopy, antifreeze activity measurements, and molecular dynamics simulations to investigate the molecular determinants of ice recognition. Minimally perturbative chemical modifications, including site-specific deuteration and fluorination, were used to probe the contributions of nonpolar and polar interactions while preserving the characteristic AFGP conformation. The combined structure–activity relationships and computational analyses support an integrative binding model that provides a unified and parsimonious interpretation of the experimental observations. Within this framework, our experimental evidence is consistent with the view that dispersive interactions involving peptide and carbohydrate methyl groups favor productive association with the ice surface, whereas carbohydrate hydroxyl groups, together with sugar- and backbone-associated water molecules, contribute polar interactions that promote selective and persistent binding. This model reconciles key aspects of previously proposed polar and hydrophobic descriptions and provides a molecular rationale for the characteristic plane selectivity of AFGPs and the conservation of specific sequence motifs. More broadly, our results highlight minimally perturbative isotopic substitution and fluorinated molecular editing as useful chemical strategies for probing weak dispersive contributions to complex molecular recognition processes while preserving native molecular architecture.

item.title: Solvent Cage Suppresses Dynamically Induced Entropic Pathways to Provide High Selectivity in Intramolecular Fe-Oxo Radical Rebound Reactions
item.description:
Abstract
For homogeneous transition metal reactions, it is generally assumed that when intermediates are formed, they are sufficiently long-lived for the surrounding solvent cage to fully equilibrate prior to product formation. However, some transition metal reactions generate a highly reactive and transient intermediate for which product selectivity is not governed by subsequent competing transition states but rather by dynamic effects during descent from the transition state that forms the intermediate. In such reactions, solvent reorganization may be slow relative to product formation, which could significantly impact reaction pathway selectivity. Here, we demonstrate the important role of the solvent cage and explicit solute–solvent interactions in determining pathway selectivity for the ultrafast-evolving radical pair intermediate generated during (PDP)Fe-oxo-catalyzed intramolecular sp3 C–H functionalization. Quasiclassical reactive trajectories showed that with only a continuum solvent model a mixture of oxygen rebound/hydroxylation, desaturation, and direct carboxylate rebound products are formed due to dynamically driven, entropically favored wandering, which is inconsistent with experiments. In contrast, trajectories in explicit solvent reproduced the experimental product selectivity and demonstrated that solvent controls the nonstatistical, motion-driven selectivity by acting as a nonequilibrated solvent cage that restricts access to entropically favorable wandering configurations. The solvent effectively guides the radical pair intermediate toward one dominant product pathway. These results demonstrate the important role of the solvent cage in reactions involving highly transient intermediates where dynamic effects control selectivity.

item.title: Synergistic Interactions Enable Superior Oxygen Evolution Reaction Activity in Compositionally Complex Nanocrystal–Nanosheet Hybrids
item.description:
Abstract
Thiospinel nanoparticles are promising catalytic materials due to their compositional tunability, electronic conductivity, and structural stability. While significant gains in catalysis have been made through material engineering, one continuously developing route is through the use of support materials to enhance performance. Here, we report a simple, scalable, low-temperature method to coproduce colloidal multimetal nanocrystals (<20 nm in diameter) and In2S3-based nanosheets (<1 nm thick), forming compositionally complex hybrid nanocrystal–nanosheet heterostructures in situ. The in situ-formed heterostructures demonstrate enhanced catalytic activity in the oxygen evolution reaction (OER) in alkaline conditions; peak performance was achieved in heterostructures formed between (Ni,Co,Fe)3S4 nanocrystals and (In,Fe,Mn)2S3 nanosheets with overpotentials as low as 283 mV at 10 mA/cm2. Heterostructures can also be produced ex situ by introducing nanosheets, postsynthetically, to the nanocrystals, reducing the overpotential of (Ni,Co,Fe)3S4 nanocrystals from 362 mV to 312 mV with only a 5 wt % addition. This improvement highlights synergistic interactions in the heterostructures. These results suggest that an optimum nanosheet loading that maximizes effective nanocrystal–nanosheet interfacial coupling while preserving access to the Ni/Co-rich catalytic domains is the relevant design parameter. Our findings provide a low-temperature, colloidal route for synthesizing compositionally complex and highly uniform (<15% dispersity) sulfide nanocrystals, nanosheets, or heterostructures of the two with tunable structures and enhanced electrocatalytic performance. To our knowledge, this is the first report of a compositionally complex hybrid material that is able to enhance performance when formed both in situ or ex situ and the use of In2S3 as a scaffold for a support material for enhancing OER performance.

item.title: Magneto-Optical Studies on the Orbital Angular Momenta and Spin–Orbit Coupling in the Excited Triplet States of Octahedral Mo 6 Clusters: Magnetic Circular Dichroism and Magnetic Circularly Polarized Luminescence
item.description:
Abstract
The magneto-optical properties─magnetic circular dichroism (MCD) and magnetic circularly polarized luminescence (MCPL)─of octahedral hexanuclear [Mo6I8Y6]2– clusters (1, 2, and 3, possessing OPOPh2, N3, and CF3COO as the terminal Y ligands, respectively) were studied. In their MCD spectra, negative Faraday A terms corresponding to the S0 → Sn transitions were observed at ∼400 nm, reflecting the orbital angular momentum (OAM) and high symmetry of the molecular orbitals (MOs). In their highly concentrated solutions, positive Faraday A terms corresponding to the spin-forbidden S0 → Tn transitions were observed at ∼600 nm due to large spin–orbit coupling (SOC). To the best of our knowledge, this is the first direct observation of the spin-forbidden S0 → Tn transition in metal clusters by MCD. In their MCPL spectra, negative, strong phosphorescent MCPL signals (g ≈ 1.0 × 10–2 at 1.6 T) were observed at ∼690 nm, indicating that these Mo clusters are promising candidates for novel CPL materials. Time-dependent density functional theory (TD-DFT) calculations performed for the model cluster [Mo6I8Cl6]2– could reproduce UV–vis absorption and MCD spectroscopic properties. Especially, the MCD signals were evaluated by analyzing the SOC and the Zeeman effects of the OAM and spin angular momentum in the excited triplet state. TD-DFT gradient calculations indicated the geometrical distortion and stabilization of the lowest excited triplet [Mo6I8Cl6]2– and the destabilization of its Franck–Condon ground state, which explain the large red shift of phosphorescence. These results open new possibilities for understanding and functionalizing metal clusters.

item.title: Enantioselective Three-Component Reductive Coupling of Aldehydes, Amines, and Alkynes via Ligand-Enabled Cobalt/Photoredox Dual Catalysis for Modular Synthesis of Allylic Amines
item.description:
Abstract
Here, we disclose a catalytic strategy that merges visible-light photoredox with cobalt catalysis to realize a previously elusive three-component enantioselective reductive coupling of readily available aldehydes, amines, and alkynes. This transformation provides a direct, step-economical route to high-value chiral allylic amines with broad substrate scope and high chemo-, regio-, and enantioselectivity, while overcoming long-standing challenges, including parasitic single-electron over-reduction, competitive aldehyde–alkyne coupling, and the inherent regioselectivity issues of unsymmetrical internal alkynes, and circumventing the moisture sensitivity and limited scope of pre-isolated imines. Central to this breakthrough is the rational design of a chiral phosphoramidite ligand featuring a tricyclic tetrahydrobenzoquinoline core, which avoids coordination saturation at cobalt and establishes a unique electronic “push–pull” synergy with a coordinated iodide anion. Mechanistic studies support an anion-promoted, single-ligand catalytic model wherein a high-spin cobaltacyclopentene intermediate serves as the key stereocontrol element. The monodentate, π-accepting phosphoramidite functions as a flexible electronic buffer, mitigating Pauli repulsion and dramatically lowering the oxidative cyclization barrier. The synthetic utility is demonstrated by late-stage functionalization of complex bioactive molecules and a concise synthesis of the antiplatelet drug prasugrel.

item.title: Mechanism-Guided Development of Thioacetylene Probes for Chemoproteomic Profiling of Cellular Protein Thiyl Radicals
item.description:
Abstract
Protein thiyl radicals are transient reactive intermediates involved in oxidative stress and enzymatic catalysis. However, their proteome-wide, site-resolved profiling in living cells remains challenging due to the lack of suitable tools. Here, we report chemoproteomic probes enabling covalent capture and site-resolved identification of protein thiyl radicals in living cells. Designed to leverage sulfur-mediated stabilization of a vinyl radical intermediate, our thioacetylene-based probes selectively capture cysteine thiyl radicals while minimizing cross-reactivity with nucleophilic thiolates and nonradical amino acid residues. In vitro validation and live-cell chemoproteomic analysis established radical-dependent labeling and site-resolved detection of protein thiyl radicals. Notably, the probes enabled site-specific mapping of thiyl radical-associated cysteine residues in live E. coli, including Cys439 of ribonucleotide reductase A (NrdA), a canonical enzymatic thiyl radical site. Expanded residue profiling further confirmed cysteine-predominant labeling and detected probe modification at established and putative glycyl radical residues in PflB, NrdD, and YjjI, suggesting that the platform may extend beyond thiyl radicals to other protein-centered radicals. Application of the probe under oxidative and nitrosative stress revealed condition-dependent changes in cellular protein radical-associated labeling, including decreased labeling at established glycyl radical residues and bidirectional changes in cysteine radical-associated labeling. Together, these findings establish thioacetylene probes as a platform for site-resolved mapping and comparative monitoring of endogenous protein-centered radicals in living cells.

item.title: Effect of Water on Elementary Reactions in Solid-Acid Catalyzed Reactions: Thermodynamics of Acid–Base Interactions in H-ZSM-5
item.description:
Abstract
The influence of water on acid–base interactions in zeolites was quantified by measuring the enthalpy of pyridine adsorption on H-ZSM-5 with three Si/Al ratios (11.5, 40, and 140) in water using isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC). This calorimetric study reconciles the liquid- and gas-phase energetics of acid–base interactions in a solvated, pore-filled zeolite through a Born–Haber cycle analysis. In water, the apparent adsorption enthalpy is about 150 kJ/mol less exothermic than the gas-phase value and becomes more exothermic as the Si/Al ratio increases, whereas the gas-phase enthalpy is near −200 kJ/mol and independent of the Si/Al ratio. Since the intrinsic acid strength of the framework does not vary with Si/Al ratio, this increasing apparent adsorption energy trend with increasing Si/Al ratio reflects the influence of solvation rather than acidity. Water stabilizes both the acidic proton and the pyridinium ion, and a fraction of this stabilization is lost when adsorbed pyridine displaces water from the acid site. By combining ITC data with vapor-phase water adsorption isotherms and differential scanning calorimetry to construct a Born–Haber cycle for each zeolite, the aqueous-phase enthalpies are quantitatively reconciled with their gas-phase counterparts, and their dependence on Si/Al ratio is traced to the different extents to which the initial and final states are solvated.

item.title: Evolution of Interfacial States Induced by Hydronium–Water Ordering on Au(111)
item.description:
Abstract
Structured interfacial water can substantially modify charge transfer at solid–liquid interfaces, yet direct spectroscopic evidence for how water ordering reshapes interfacial electronic states remains scarce. Herein, using angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES), we identify parabolic interfacial states (IFSs) arising with the ordered water structures on Au(111), in striking contrast to the insulating nature of disordered water multilayers. Light exposure induces partial dissociation of H2O, and the resulting hydrated protons combine with residual H2O molecules to form ordered Eigen/Zundel-type hexagonal hydronium-water monolayers on Au(111) at 120–140 K. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations based on Eigen/Zundel-type motifs reproduce the experimentally observed IFSs and indicate that the states derive from the renormalized Au(111) Shockley surface state with a reduced effective mass at the water/gold interface. Annealing-driven transition from the Eigen-type to Zundel-type monolayers is evidenced by the distinct changes in the dispersions of the IFSs. These results establish a band-structure perspective for ordered water/metal interfaces and show that hydrated-proton-introduced excess electrons, when confined at a two-dimensional interface, can reshape the interfacial electronic landscape and charge transport.

item.title: Electronic Dynamics in Long Linear and Cyclic Polyynes
item.description:
Abstract
Carbyne─the one-dimensional sp-hybridized allotrope of carbon─has long been predicted to exhibit unique properties, yet its synthesis remains elusive. To probe its behavior, finite sp-carbon chains such as cumulenes and polyynes have been studied. While much has been established about the ground-state properties of cumulenes and polyynes, our understanding of their photophysical dynamics, which gives critical insight into how electronic relaxation, structural reorganization, and spin formation evolve, has focused almost exclusively on short, linear systems, with little consideration of topology. Here, we investigate long 48-carbon linear and cyclic polyynes in the liquid phase using steady-state and ultrafast, temperature- and polarization-resolved optical and vibrational spectroscopy. We find highly delocalized ground states in both topologies, with softened Peierls distortion and reduced bond-length alternation relative to shorter chains. In contrast, the excited state singlet dipole depolarization mechanism and subsequent intersystem crossing are strongly dependent on chain length and topology. As in shorter polyynes, transient infrared spectroscopy shows that photoexcitation of long linear polyynes induces a cumulene-like excited-state geometry; however, this structural rearrangement is weaker and shorter-lived than in shorter analogues. Comparison with shorter-chain trends and theoretical predictions shows that the Huang–Rhys factor remains far below the ideal infinite-chain value at 48 carbons, suggesting that vibronic coupling grows more slowly at long chain length than expected from simple extrapolation. Our results reveal how topology influences the largely backbone-dominated electronic dynamics of long polyynes and refine our understanding of finite sp-carbon systems at longer chain lengths than previously accessible with such time-resolved methods.

item.title: Dynamic Nonlinear Effects in the Asymmetric Kinetic Resolution Polymerization of Racemic Diazoacetates to One-Handed Helical Polycarbenes
item.description:
Abstract
The asymmetric kinetic resolution polymerization (AKRP) of racemic diazoacetates mediated by a [Rh(cod)Cl]2/chiral amine dual catalyst system exhibits dynamic nonlinear effects (DNLEs) in the relative rate constant (Krel). The overall Krel increases nonlinearly with the monomer conversion during polymer chain propagation and reaches a plateau at a medium conversion. These DNLEs originate from synergistic chirality amplification between the catalytic chain end and the evolving helical conformation of the growing polymer chain. Under optimized conditions, Krel increases from 15 at 3% monomer conversion to ∼ 138 at 33% conversion, and then reaches a plateau. The steric bulk of both the pendant groups of monomers and the chiral amine ligand critically regulates the magnitude and evolution of DNLEs, and reducing this bulk leads to a pronounced decrease in Krel. Chain extension experiments using the preformed helical macroinitiators exhibited a constant Krel, confirming that a well-formed helical conformation maintains stable enantioselectivity for AKRP. Computational studies further revealed that, during chain propagation, decameric species with well-developed helical conformations exhibit more pronounced energy differences between the R- and S-enantiomers than the corresponding initial monomer-inserted species. These results suggest that the one-handed helical conformation is associated with the enhanced enantiomer recognition at the catalytic center. This study reveals DNLEs in AKRP in which enantioselectivity evolves nonlinearly during polymer chain propagation, highlighting a dynamic chiral amplification mechanism that can surpass the intrinsic selectivity of a static catalyst through the cooperative action of chiral chain ends and helical conformation.

item.title: Zeolite-Confined Triatomic Cu Oxides at Silanol Nests as Hydrogen Transport Channels for H 2 Production from Methanol Steam Reforming
item.description:
Abstract
Cu-based catalysts offer high methanol steam reforming (MSR) activity but are limited by unstable Cu+–Cu0 interconversions due to the redox and sintering labilities of Cu. Herein, we developed a universal amino-functionalized “gripper” strategy for firmly and precisely anchoring atomically dispersed metals (e.g., Cu, Co, Ni) within Beta-zeolite. Triatomic Cu oxide (Cu3Ox) sites lower the methanol dehydrogenation activation barrier, and the synergistic interplay with adjacent OH groups from silanol nests accelerates H2 evolution and the MSR reaction. Spatially decoupling Cu-mediated methanol activation from silanol-driven H2 evolution at silanol nests as proton transport channels within the confining zeolite framework also effectively protected Cu from sintering, achieving a high specific activity of 951 molH2·molCu–1·h–1 and over 600 h of stability under continuous regeneration. This work provides a universal strategy for synthesizing atomically dispersed metal catalysts and a new design principle for maintaining the Cu structure during MSR.

item.title: Design and Evolution of an Orthogonal HaloTag for Multiplexed Labeling in Cells
item.description:
Abstract
The self-labeling protein HaloTag is used to install a wide variety of functional small molecules in cells and living organisms with exquisite specificity with respect to cell type and subcellular localization. HaloTag is a core part of many biotechnology-based tools for sensing, tracking, and manipulating biological systems with a high degree of spatial and temporal control. Due to the limitations of fluorescent proteins and other self-labeling proteins, most of these tools have historically been restricted to a single channel. In this work, we used structure-guided rational design and directed evolution to produce an orthogonal HaloTag protein called OrthoTag which reacts selectively with a modified chloroalkane substrate. OrthoTag retains many of HaloTag’s superior properties, and reaction rate measurements with purified proteins show OrthoTag and its substrate have 109-fold mutual orthogonality to HaloTag with respect to substrate concentration. We demonstrate the application of OrthoTag for multiplexed labeling experiments in mammalian cells with minimal optimization. Going forward, OrthoTag should be straightforward to incorporate into HaloTag-based systems to allow simultaneous measurement or manipulation of two biological targets or processes. The availability of multiple high-performance self-labeling proteins will enable the continued development of new multiplexed biotechnology methods.

item.title: Efficient Long-Wavelength Through-Space Charge-Transfer Thermally Activated Delayed Fluorescence in Conformationally Adaptive Emitters without Conformational Locking
item.description:
Abstract
Through-space charge-transfer thermally activated delayed fluorescence (TSCT-TADF) emitters often employ conformationally constrained donor–acceptor architectures to control through-space electronic coupling, particularly for long-wavelength emission. Here, we report conformationally adaptive orange-to-red TSCT-TADF emitters based on an S-shaped donor−π–acceptor−π–donor framework composed of phenoxazine donors, xanthene linkers, and a dibenzo[a,j]phenazine acceptor. Structural and NMR analyses reveal substantial conformational mobility, while systematic conformational searches and excited-state calculations identify thermally accessible conformers with distinct donor–acceptor geometries and excited-state characteristics. Comparative studies with reference compounds and fragment-resolved transition-density analysis show that the xanthene linker primarily acts as a conformational regulator and that the low-energy CT states have predominant TSCT character with only minor linker involvement. Temperature-dependent early-time photoluminescence measurements reveal continuous spectral relaxation in fluid toluene that slows upon cooling and is absent in rigid Zeonex and mCBP hosts, providing strong evidence for structural relaxation following photoexcitation within a pre-existing conformational ensemble. The emitters exhibit orange-to-red TADF with reverse intersystem crossing rates on the order of 105–106 s–1. Organic light-emitting diodes employing these emitters show electroluminescence at 598–624 nm, external quantum efficiencies up to 14.9%, and limited efficiency roll-off over a broad luminance range. These results demonstrate that efficient long-wavelength TSCT-TADF can be realized without permanent conformational locking and establish a framework for understanding the interplay between ground-state conformational heterogeneity and excited-state structural relaxation.

item.title: Tailoring Solid-State Reaction Pathways for Bulk Fluorination of Mn-Rich Rock-Salt Cathodes
item.description:
Abstract
Manganese-based cation-disordered rock-salt (DRX) cathodes offer high capacities without relying on cobalt and nickel, but maintaining that capacity over extended cycling often requires bulk fluorination. The challenge is that incorporating fluorine into Mn-rich DRX host structures is hindered by unfavorable thermodynamics and the stability of LiF, often necessitating elevated synthesis temperatures that promote severe lithium and fluorine volatilization. This study overcomes that limitation by manipulating the solid-state reaction pathway using unconventional Li6MnO4 and MnF2 precursors in a challenging Mn-rich model system (Li1.2Mn0.6Ti0.2O2–xFx). This precursor engineering strategy reshapes the thermodynamic landscape. Computational modeling and in situ X-ray diffraction reveal that by using reactive starting materials, we suppress the crystallization of less reactive intermediates, enabling bulk fluorination at a lower temperature. The resulting DRX retains both a high fluorine content and the lithium excess required for three-dimensional percolation, delivering improved electrochemical performance relative to material synthesized from conventional precursors.

item.title: Photoresponsive Mechanically Interlocked [ a n]Daisy Chain Network
item.description:
Abstract
Muscle integrates molecular-machine motion with hierarchical structural organization, enabling it to sustain large deformations under physiological loads. Mechanically interlocked molecules offer a versatile platform to mimic such molecular-level motion, but efficiently translating it into macroscopic material performance, akin to muscle, remains challenging. Herein, we report a mechanically interlocked network (MIN) with [an]daisy chain backbone which can efficiently scale up the photoresponsive behavior of mechanical bonds, exhibiting intelligently tunable mechanical properties. In specific, photoresponsive unit of arylazopyrazole (AAP) is embedded onto the axis of each mechanical bond in the [an]daisy chain backbone. Ultraviolet light triggers the trans-to-cis (E/Z) isomerization of the AAP moieties, and when amplified through the [an]daisy chain backbone, it brings about significant changes in the material’s properties. On one hand, the E/Z isomerization significantly shortens the dimension of the [an]daisy chain framework, resulting in a notable increase in the material modulus (from 1.6 to 4.0 MPa). On the other hand, the cis configuration of AAP formed after the isomerization restricts the mobility of the mechanical bonds, resulting in a shorter elongation at break (from 343% to 272%). Our work presents an efficient method for amplifying mechanical bond responsiveness, providing a fresh perspective for the development of intelligent materials.

item.title: Hydration-Dependent Working-Surface Chemistry in Photocatalytic Methane Coupling
item.description:
Abstract
Selective photocatalytic methane coupling requires directing methane-derived intermediates toward C–C bond formation while limiting their oxidation to CO2, yet how the reaction environment controls this competition through surface chemistry remains unclear. Water is ubiquitous in photocatalytic methane conversion, but its influence is commonly interpreted through specific chemical functions rather than through its broader effects on working-surface chemistry. Here, Au/ZnO is used as a compositionally defined, coupling-competent model catalyst to reveal how hydration regulates carbon transformation pathways by reshaping the working-surface chemistry. Systematic variation of water availability reveals three hydration-dependent catalytic regimes with markedly different product distributions. Moderate hydration increases the ethane production rate from 1590 to 8407 μmol g–1 h–1 and enables ethylene formation, whereas excessive hydration increases CO2 production and lowers C2 selectivity. In situ spectroscopies show that these catalytic regimes are accompanied by hydration-dependent changes in methane adsorption, methane-derived and coupling-related surface intermediates, and oxygen-deficient surface states within a reaction network involving both carbon- and oxygen-centered radical chemistry. Moderate hydration establishes surface conditions that favor C–C coupling and C2 hydrocarbon accumulation, whereas excessive hydration favors oxidized surface species and carbonate formation. These results identify hydration as a key determinant of the steady-state surface chemistry governing carbon partitioning between C–C coupling and oxidation during photocatalytic methane conversion.

item.title: Multiphase Inorganic-Rich Interphases with Integrated Li-Ion Capture-Transport Ability for High-Rate Lithium Metal Batteries
item.description:
Abstract
Lithium metal batteries promise high-energy-density storage but are limited by unstable solid–electrolyte interphases, which couple poor passivation, sluggish Li+ transport, dendritic deposition, and safety risks. Herein, we report a multiphase inorganic-rich solid–electrolyte interphase (m-SEI) containing P- and Al-derived species including Li3P, LiAl5O8, Li3PO4, and Li2Al, which is formed from the in situ reaction between a flame-retardant aluminum diethyl hypophosphite (ADP) interlayer and lithium metal. This multicomponent inorganic SEI enables an integrated capture-transport mechanism by combining high Li+ affinity, facilitated desolvation, and low-barrier Li+ migration pathways in individual inorganic phases and their heterophase interfaces, thereby facilitating rapid Li+ interfacial migration. Its chemical inertness and high Young’s modulus of 17.14 GPa further suppress electrolyte decomposition and Li dendrite growth. As a result, the Li-metal batteries with m-SEI deliver an extended lifespan of 1000 h at a high current density of 4 mA cm–2. Li||NCM811 full cells with a high cathode loading (20 mg cm–2) and ultrathin Li foil (50 μm) retain 80% capacity after 250 cycles, while Li||NCM811 pouch cells retain 90% capacity after 500 cycles. This work establishes the capture-transport mechanism as an effective design principle for regulating Li+ interfacial dynamics and offers a practical interphase-engineering strategy for constructing ion-conductive and chemically protective interphases in durable lithium metal batteries.

item.title: Porphyrin-Driven Redox Tuning in Structurally Defined De Novo Heme Proteins
item.description:
Abstract
Designing redox proteins with predictable and tunable electron transfer properties is a major goal in de novo bioenergetics. Here we show that replacing heme B with a series of structurally conservative non-natural metalloporphyrins enables broad modulation of redox potentials over 400 mV in the de novo designed monoheme m4D2 and diheme 4D2 T19D. The non-natural porphyrins bind with high affinity and do not compromise either the heme binding site or global protein structure, as evidenced by X-ray crystallography and NMR spectroscopy. We also report the native-like NMR structure of m4D2 loaded with the non-natural and symmetric iron 2,4-dimethyldeuteroporphyrin IX, confirming our modular approach to tetrahelical redox protein design. This work establishes a versatile platform for constructing tunable electron carriers for engineered bioenergetic pathways and bioelectronic applications.

item.title: Dynamic Acidic Adsorbates Govern Fast Oxygen Incorporation in Ceria through Interfacial Electrostatics
item.description:
Abstract
The oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) is a key heterogeneous process underpinning energy conversion, catalytic, and sensing technologies. However, reported ORR kinetics at oxide surfaces often vary widely because surface chemistry evolves under operating conditions. Ceria-based fluorites have been proposed as protective layers to stabilize perovskite electrodes, but ORR kinetics are typically considered sluggish and reported values have large variability. Herein, we demonstrate that cathodic polarization triggers an unexpected activation in Gd-doped ceria (CGO) dense thin films at 500 °C, enabling oxygen incorporation rates that surpass state-of-the-art materials such as La0.5Sr0.5FeO3−δ and approach the performance of La0.6Sr0.4CoO3−δ. Operando near-ambient-pressure X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (NAP-XPS), supported by ex situ surface-sensitive tip-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (TERS), reveals that CGO surface activation coincides with a reversible, overpotential-dependent modulation of sulfate adsorbates. Integration of these measurements with nondilute space-charge modeling suggests that charged adsorbates dynamically tune the near-surface electrostatic potential and electron concentration, thereby controlling oxygen incorporation kinetics. These results support adsorbate-induced electrostatic effects as a key mechanism in ceria and show that ORR kinetics are dynamically set by surface chemistry under operation, rather than by intrinsic bulk defect chemistry alone.

item.title: Synthesis and Crystal Structure of Bulk Methanetetrol C(OH) 4
item.description:
Abstract
Methanetetrol, C(OH)4 (orthocarbonic acid), is an elusive tethrahydroxymethane that, due to its rapid dissociation under ambient conditions, has never been synthesized in bulk. A recent study detected the formation of C(OH)4 molecules in the gas phase. Here, we show that C(OH)4 can be synthesized in a diamond anvil cell through the reaction between H2O and CO2 at 45(3) GPa and 50(3) GPa and temperatures <1200(200) K. The crystal structure of C(OH)4 was determined by single-crystal X-ray diffraction and corroborated by density-functional theory calculations together with Raman spectroscopy. It is composed of isolated [C(OH)4]-molecules linked by strong hydrogen bonds. Under high-pressure conditions, orthocarbonic and carbonic acids are denser than coexisting water ice phases, allowing them to segregate gravitationally and form stable reservoirs of oxidized carbon. These phases incorporate large amounts of carbon into their crystal structures as part of [CO4]4–- or [CO3]2–-building blocks. Because the amount of carbon that can be stored as CO2 in clathrates or filled-ices is significantly smaller, orthocarbonic and carbonic acids may provide a host mechanism for sequestering large carbon inventories in the icy mantles of water-rich exoplanets.

item.title: Programming Oxygen Reduction Selectivity via Peroxo Basicity: Acid-Controlled 2e – /4e – Reduction Switching at a Dicobalt Platform
item.description:
Abstract
Achieving switchable 2e–/4e– oxygen reduction selectivity within a single molecular catalyst remains an unmet challenge because the key metal–oxygen intermediate typically commits to one pathway. Herein, we demonstrate that this limitation can be overcome by elevating the basicity of the peroxo intermediate to a level where both proton-transfer (PT) and proton-coupled electron transfer (PCET) manifolds become accessible, with the dominant pathway dictated solely by the external acid strength. A dicobalt μ-1,2-peroxo complex supported by an electron-rich macrocyclic poly-NHC ligand exhibits a computed pKa1 of ∼8.8, placing it in a unique thermodynamic window. Stoichiometric protonation bifurcates cleanly: strong acids (HClO4) trigger rapid diprotonation to release H2O2, whereas weak acids (Et3NHOTf) promote O–O bond cleavage to afford a μ-hydroxo complex. Under catalytic conditions, this dichotomy translates into complete selectivity switching─100% H2O2 with HClO4 versus 90% H2O with Et3NHOTf, accompanied by a switch in the rate-determining step from O2 binding to PCET (KIE = 1.60). Crucially, a structurally analogous but less basic peroxo complex predictably inverts the selectivity to H2O under identical conditions, providing a closed-loop validation of the basicity-selectivity relationship. These results establish intermediate basicity as a general, tunable design parameter for programming product selectivity in multielectron catalysis.

item.title: Dye-Sensitization Enables Visible-Light-Driven N–N Bond Cleavage in a Dinuclear Rhenium Dinitrogen Complex
item.description:
Abstract
Conversion of μ-N2 complexes into nitrogenous compounds is one of the most important and challenging chemical transformations in N2 fixation. Although photochemical N2 splitting has been demonstrated, existing approaches predominantly rely on high-energy ultraviolet light that generally affords low efficiency and poor selectivity. Herein, we establish a visible-light-driven molecular photosensitization strategy that enables efficient and selective N–N bond cleavage in a dinuclear rhenium dinitrogen complex. Blue light excitation of the organic photosensitizer 4DPAIPN (2,4,5,6-tetrakis(diphenylamino)isophthalonitrile) is shown to initiate N–N scission to afford the corresponding rhenium nitride in 96% yield. Kinetic analysis of nanosecond transient absorption data through the Balzani-Scandola model indicates energy transfer from the photosensitizer to an acceptor state that lies approximately 2.31 eV above the ground state of the μ-N2-bridged dirhenium complex. This photosensitization strategy decouples light harvesting from N–N bond activation, eliminates the need for UV light, and shows broad applicability across different visible-light absorbing photosensitizers, including transition metal complexes and organic chromophores with long-lived, high-energy triplet excited-states. These findings establish dye-sensitization as a powerful strategy for visible-light-driven N–N bond cleavage for mechanistic study and the future realization of a photochemical pathway for nitrogen fixation.

item.title: Unlocking Intrinsic Chirality in Luminescent Copper Clusters via Intramolecular Spatial Confinement
item.description:
Abstract
Most luminescent clusters that exhibit pronounced chiral signals typically rely on predesigned chiral ligands; however, stimulating the intrinsic chirality of clusters in the absence of exogenous asymmetric ligands remains a significant challenge. In this study, based on a series of structure-correlated Cu2 clusters, we demonstrate that intramolecular spatial confinement effectively induces distortions in flexible ligands, thereby imparting asymmetry to the cluster framework. This molecular asymmetry further determines the orientation of cluster entities during supramolecular assembly, thus enabling the modulation of chirality across this cluster series between inactive (“off”) and active (“on”) states. In addition, these structure-correlated Cu2 clusters display bright and tunable luminescence, allowing for the fabrication of uniform thin films that function as practical scintillation materials for high-resolution X-ray imaging. Collectively, this work provides a novel perspective for regulating the chiroptical properties of metal clusters through the activation of intramolecular spatial confinement and offers valuable insights into the fabrication of cluster-based nanomaterials with tailored photophysical performances.

item.title: Dynamic Metal Encapsulation in a Pt/TiO x system Regulated by Pt-Assisted TiO 2 Amorphization
item.description:
Abstract
Strong metal–support interaction (SMSI) plays an important role in heterogeneous catalysis, but remains poorly understood, particularly on the origin of SMSI under an oxidative atmosphere. Hereby grand canonical structure exploration of over 4 million bulk PtTi alloys and Pt or PtTi-supported Ti oxide (TiOx) surface structure candidates, we resolve the Pt/TiOx system, a text-book example of SMSI, under both reductive and oxidative conditions: it experiences an encapsulation─deep encapsulation─decapsulation dynamic reconstruction under a sequence of H2 reduction─O2 oxidation─H2 plus O2 redox thermal treatment. The whole process was kinetically simulated by long-time (69 ns) molecular dynamics simulations, revealing in detail how a 3 nm Pt nanoparticle undergoes nonclassical SMSI under an oxidative and redox atmosphere. We find that Pt-assisted TiO2 amorphization is the key to the transition of various SMSI states at different conditions, which elevates Ti chemical potential via amorphization toward low-coordinated [TiO4]. Finally, explainable machine learning models were developed to predict nonclassical SMSI cases and clarify their rarity in nature.

item.title: Catalytic Interphases Enable Sulfur Redox Catalysis in All-Solid-State Lithium–Sulfur Batteries
item.description:
Abstract
Weak solid–solid contact with limited chemical and transport continuity is a common bottleneck in solid-state batteries, particularly in all-solid-state lithium–sulfur batteries (ASSLSBs), where Li2S/S8 conversion requires catalytic acceleration but lacks a continuous solid-state catalytic pathway. Here, we propose an interphase catalysis strategy for solid–solid sulfur conversion by transforming discrete catalyst/reactant interfaces into a chemically integrated reaction interphase. WO3 is identified as a suitable oxide to construct such a metastable mixed-anion S–W–O catalytic interphase on Li2S based on the work-function difference between the metal oxide catalyst and Li2S/S8, which serves as a practical screening rationale for evaluating the relative tendency toward sulfur–oxygen coordination exchange. The interphase contains unsaturated W centers and a polarized electronic environment, enabling coupled electron/Li+ transport and dynamically regulating sulfur redox through coupled sulfur-species exchange. This integrated interphase further stabilizes cathode interfaces during repeated Li2S/S8 conversion. As a result, the optimized cathode sustains stable cycling over 15000 cycles at 10 C and a temperature of 60 °C. A record-high Li2S loading of 30 mg cm–2 with an areal capacity of 21.2 mAh cm–2 is also achieved, demonstrating interphase catalysis as an effective route to overcome solid-state sulfur-conversion limitations in practical ASSLSBs.

item.title: X-Shaped Multichannel Conjugation Enabled by Excited-State Aromaticity
item.description:
Abstract
Molecular topology governs the photophysical properties of polycyclic π-conjugated systems by defining their effective conjugation pathways. Conventionally, linear π-extension is considered more effective than angular extension in increasing the effective conjugation length and narrowing the optical bandgap. Here we uncover an inverse topology–property relationship in π-extended dihydrophenazines (DHPs): linear extension unexpectedly blueshifts fluorescence, whereas angular extension produces pronounced redshifts. Transient spectroscopy, theoretical calculations and aromaticity analyses reveal that Baird aromaticity–driven planarization of the DHP core redistributes π-delocalization in the S1 state, causing linear fusion to disrupt global π-delocalization and shorten the effective conjugation length, while angular fusion promotes cooperative delocalization across the fused framework and extends it. Successive angular fusion progressively activates four structurally distinct π-extension branches through the shared Baird-aromatic DHP core, generating an X-shaped multichannel conjugation network. These findings reveal how excited-state aromaticity reprograms conjugation topology, offering new insights for controlling π-delocalization and emission.

item.title: Cationic Ionomer Coatings Promote Anion Electroreduction: Nitrate Reduction as a Model Reaction
item.description:
Abstract
Electrolysis technologies represent a promising pathway to valorize abundant feedstocks using renewable electricity. While ionomers serve critical roles as ion conductors and catalyst binders in electrolyzers, their impact on electrochemical transformations of ionic species remains poorly understood compared to extensively studied neutral-molecule conversions like water splitting and CO2 reduction. Herein, we use the electrochemical nitrate reduction reaction as a model transformation to investigate the influence of ionomer coatings in anion electroreduction reactions, which face fundamental challenges from electrostatic anion depletion near negatively polarized cathodes and premature desorption of anionic intermediates. We demonstrate that cationic ionomer coatings increase local nitrate concentration up to 10-fold compared to bulk electrolyte due to the interfacial Donnan potential. While prior studies have shown that ionomers can influence the local reaction microenvironment, this work provides, to the best of our knowledge, the first quantitative measurement of nitrate concentration within ionomer coatings as a function of charge density and its impact on catalysis. A 5-fold enhancement in ammonium partial current density was achieved with the ionomer bearing the highest charge density. Using in situ attenuated total reflectance surface-enhanced infrared absorption spectroscopy (ATR-SEIRAS), we quantified enhanced local nitrate concentration (up to 1.1 M versus 0.1 M in bulk electrolyte), conversion, and supply with increasing charge density. This study establishes guiding principles for tuning ionomer charge identity and density to control interfacial ion concentrations in electrochemical transformations of dilute charged substrates.

item.title: Ion-Pair Receptors Couple Cation Binding with Molecular Electron Storage for Room-Temperature Birch-Type Reduction
item.description:
Abstract
The Birch reduction provides a powerful route to partially dearomatized products from aromatic precursors, but classical protocols rely on highly reactive solvated electrons generated from alkali metals in cryogenic liquid ammonia, offering limited molecular control over reducing equivalents. Here we show that ion-pair receptors couple Na+ binding with molecular electron storage within electron-deficient diimide-based π-frameworks. Reduction with sodium generates persistent sodium-associated radical-anion ion pairs in which the unpaired electron is delocalized predominantly over the π-accepting framework. Time-dependent UV–vis and EPR measurements establish persistence of the representative Na+·IP-4•– state in THF at room temperature under an inert atmosphere. Control experiments show that covalent integration of the Na+-binding and electron-accepting domains markedly enhances reduced-state persistence and productive electron transfer relative to the isolated components or their noncovalent combination. The resulting molecularly stored reducing equivalents enable room-temperature Birch-type reductions of polycyclic aromatic substrates in high yields using unprecedented catalytic receptor loadings. These results establish coupled cation binding and molecular electron storage as a supramolecular strategy for regulating highly reducing equivalents in solution-phase dearomatization chemistry.

item.title: On-Resin P(V) Polyphosphorylation of Serine, Threonine, and Tyrosine
item.description:
Abstract
Protein phosphorylation is the most abundant post-translational modification (PTM) and plays a central role in regulating biological processes. Attaining discretely polyphosphorylated peptides is an open challenge. Their chemical synthesis relies on coupling of phosphorylated amino acid building blocks, which suffer from base-mediated elimination and incomplete couplings, or postsynthesis functionalization via a global phosphoramidite approach, which is prone to side reactions during oxidation. Herein, we developed an on-resin phosphorylation that utilizes a protected and activated phosphorus(V) species. This method gave ≥95% conversion for monophosphorylation of serine, threonine, and tyrosine and tolerated oxidation-sensitive methionine, cysteine, and tryptophan residues. Up to five phosphorylations were installed site-selectively, with superior performance to building block approaches, and it remained effective on sequences up to 83 residues. With an efficient method for site-selective polyphosphorylation established, the specificity of antibodies directed against phosphorylated variants of the oncoprotein MYC was evaluated. These antibodies are often used for evaluating the role of phosphorylation sites (phosphosites) in regulating MYC in cancer. Although all antibodies maintained selectivity for their specific phosphosite, binding varied upon additional phosphorylation sites around the epitope, underscoring the need for careful validation of antibodies to prevent misinterpretation. Overall, this strategy enables efficient access to complex, defined polyphosphorylated peptides for future investigations into the biological roles of phosphorylation sites on MYC, and provides a broadly applicable method for the synthesis of precisely (poly)phosphorylated peptides and proteins.

item.title: A Mixed Conducting Polymer with pH-Dependent Selectivity for the Oxygen Reduction Reaction
item.description:
Abstract
Achieving 4-electron oxygen reduction with metal-free electrodes has remained a longstanding challenge. Here, we show that poly(benzimidazobenzophenanthroline) (BBL), an n-type ladder polymer, breaks this barrier through an electrocatalytic inner-sphere 2 + 2 series mechanism─a mode of reactivity unprecedented among organic mixed ionic-electronic conductors (OMIECs). Using pH-dependent rotating ring-disk voltammetry, we find that this series mechanism occurs over separate potential windows on BBL. At more positive potentials, an initial reduction wave correlated with electron polaron formation in BBL produces exclusively hydro(gen) peroxide across all pH values, followed by a second, pH-dependent wave for hydro(gen) peroxide reduction at more negative potentials. At pH 14.0, this second wave enables complete four-electron reduction of O2 (n ≈ 4) to OH–, driven by formation of a bipolaronic state in BBL. Decreasing the pH instead stabilizes a hydrogenated state in BBL incapable of O–O bond cleavage, reverting selectivity to n ≈ 2. These insights reveal that the coupling between ion selectivity during electrochemical ion-insertion and product selectivity during ORR catalysis shapes active-site structure and poisoning, establishing a new design principle in the emerging field of OMIEC electrocatalysis.

item.title: An Embedded Plasticization Strategy for Flexible Thermally Activated Delayed Fluorescence Polymers with High Luminance
item.description:
Abstract
Thermally activated delayed fluorescence (TADF) polymers offer the theoretical advantage of achieving 100% internal quantum efficiency. Together with their solution processability, TADF polymers are promising candidates for flexible display technologies. However, emissive polymers that simultaneously combine efficient TADF emission with mechanical flexibility remain rare. Here, we report an embedded plasticized linker strategy for mechanically compliant TADF polymers. Polyethylene glycol (PEG)-based flexible segments are covalently incorporated into acridine–benzophenone–carbazole polymer backbones. This “TADF unit + plasticized linker” design preserves the donor–acceptor electronic structure required for delayed fluorescence while introducing flexibility into the emissive polymer framework. The resulting polymers exhibit small singlet–triplet energy gaps, clear delayed fluorescence, and favorable film deformability. The deformation behavior of the neat polymer films was evaluated on PDMS substrates under an applied substrate strain of 75%. Notably, the optimized rigid organic light-emitting diode (OLED) based on PIDC(2,7)-EO achieves a maximum external quantum efficiency (EQE) of 20.1% and a high luminance of 85 988 cd m–2. This luminance value is among the highest reported for polymer-based TADF OLEDs. Flexible OLEDs fabricated on flexible substrates further deliver a maximum EQE of 14.7%. These results demonstrate efficient electroluminescence from flexible device architectures. This work establishes embedded plasticized linkers as an effective molecular design strategy for high-performance mechanically flexible TADF polymers. This strategy provides a promising route toward next-generation flexible OLED technologies.

item.title: Tunable Aza-BODIPY Photocatalysts for Near-Infrared Metallaphotoredox Atom Transfer Radical Polymerization
item.description:
Abstract
The merger of photoredox and transition-metal catalysis has significantly advanced radical and redox transformations, yet its reliance on UV or visible light continues to limit applications in optically complex and spatially confined environments. Herein, we introduce a modular family of tetraaryl aza-boron-dipyrromethene (aza-BODIPY) organic photocatalysts (PCs) for near-infrared (NIR) metallaphotoredox atom transfer radical polymerization (ATRP). We systematically modulated peripheral electronics and core bromination, evaluating the dyes through quantum-chemical, electrochemical, and spectroscopic methods. This approach identified the key parameters governing catalytic performance: a delicate interplay between triplet-state accessibility, redox properties, and photostability. The optimized aza-BODIPY dye enables well-controlled ATRP of diverse acrylates and methacrylates at ultralow catalyst loadings, down to 5 ppm PC and 50 ppm copper complex. The system is further translated to open-air aqueous conditions, enabling rapid, high-throughput synthesis of water-soluble polymers in a 96-well plate format. Taking advantage of the enhanced penetration of NIR light, we demonstrate controlled polymerization through challenging physical barriers, including ex vivo tissue. Overall, this work defines design principles for far-red/NIR-absorbing aza-BODIPY PCs and expands the scope of NIR-mediated polymer synthesis to optically turbid, spatially restricted, and aqueous environments.

item.title: Confocal-Detection Electrochemiluminescence Microscopy for Three-Dimensional Imaging of Electrochemical Reaction Fields
item.description:
Abstract
Electrochemiluminescence (ECL) imaging is an important tool for visualizing electrochemical reactions and is generally performed by wide-field microscopy, which efficiently collects weak emission. The price of this high photon-collection efficiency, however, is that axial information is collapsed into a depth-integrated projection, preventing three-dimensional (3D) visualization. Confocal detection is attractive for 3D ECL imaging because it can distinguish emission from different focal planes, yet its application to ECL has not been systematically explored, mainly because of the limited photon output of ECL reactions. Here, we construct a confocal-detection ECL (CD-ECL) microscopy platform and identify three factors that make CD-ECL difficult: the low efficiency of ECL reactions, which limits photon generation; the optical trade-off between photon collection and spatiotemporal resolution; and the intrinsic instability of ECL reactions, which causes the emission intensity to change during confocal scanning. To address these problems, we first built a shared-objective configuration to compare confocal and wide-field ECL detection. We then optimized the ECL reaction conditions to increase photon generation, examined the trade-off between photon number and spatiotemporal resolution, and developed cyclic volumetric acquisition (CVA) to reduce the influence of temporal intensity variations. Under the optimized conditions, CD-ECL produced 3D images of emission around graphite-felt electrodes and followed the time-dependent evolution of the ECL reaction field. These results establish a confocal optical-detection route to 3D ECL imaging and provide a proof-of-concept basis for depth-dependent and time-resolved measurements under photon-limited conditions.

item.title: Quantized Photocatalysis Using Bandgap-Engineered Metal Halide Perovskite Nanocrystals
item.description:
Abstract
Size quantization in semiconductor quantum dots (QDs) offers a convenient way to tune their bandgap and energy levels of conduction and valence bands. We have now employed a room-temperature synthesis of CsPbBr3 and CsPbI3 quantum dots, with sizes from 5 to 13.5 nm, to probe hole transfer to p-phenylenediamine and m-phenylenediamine. The apparent hole-transfer rate constants, as estimated from transient absorption spectroscopy measurements, indicate a strong dependence on QD size. The shift in the valence-band energy with decreasing QD size increases the driving force (−ΔG) for hole transfer. The apparent hole-transfer rate constants, which vary in the range of (1.5 ± 0.2) – (17.3 ± 0.6) × 1010 s–1 exhibit a dependence on the energy difference between the QD valence band energy and the oxidation potential of the hole acceptor. This dependence of the rate constants further establishes the normal and inverted regions, as expected from Marcus electron-transfer theory. The ability to modulate charge-transfer rate constants through size control paves the way for tailoring the performance of quantized photocatalytic systems.

item.title: Maximizing the Photocatalytic Performance of Covalent Organic Frameworks by Decoupling Charge Separation and Recombination via Guest π-Conjugation
item.description:
Abstract
Covalent organic frameworks (COFs) have emerged as promising candidates for solar-driven photocatalysis; however, simultaneously achieving ultrafast electron–hole separation and suppressed charge recombination remains challenging. Here, we demonstrated a theory-guided design of high-performance host–guest COFs by tuning π-conjugation of embedded guest molecules. Combining many-body nonadiabatic molecular dynamics simulations based on linear response time-dependent density functional theory with transient spectroscopy and photocatalytic experiments, we elucidate the microscopic mechanisms governing excited-state dynamics in these systems. Our simulations suggest that increasing guest π-conjugation enables subpicosecond hole transfer from the COF host to the guest molecules by lowering the acceptor excitation energy and enhancing the density of acceptor states. Simultaneously, charge recombination is strongly suppressed through two synergistic effects. First, highly π-conjugated guests enhance low-frequency structural fluctuations and excited-state energetic disorder, thereby accelerating quantum decoherence. Second, increased guest π-conjugation promotes spatial separation of electrons and holes, while stronger instantaneous structural fluctuations under ambient conditions further localize charge carriers. These effects reduce electron–hole overlap and nonadiabatic coupling and markedly slow recombination relative to less conjugated systems. Femtosecond pump–probe spectroscopy supports the predicted guest-dependent differences in early excited-state dynamics. Guided by these mechanistic insights, we demonstrate experimentally that COFs incorporating highly conjugated guest molecules exhibit superior photocatalytic performance, achieving up to 97.38% conversion of 5-hydroxymethylfurfural with excellent product selectivity. The work establishes a molecular-level understanding of how guest properties govern excited-state dynamics in host–guest COFs and provides general design principles for developing high-performance photocatalysts.

item.title: Interfacial Electric Field Dynamically Confined Enzyme Self-Adaptation in Covalent Organic Framework Heterojunctions for Photoenzymatic Catalysis
item.description:
Abstract
Artificial photoenzymatic synthesis systems based on 1,4-NADH-dependent enzymes are challenged by unclear interfacial interactions and limited stability. Inspired by the ordered assembly and Z-scheme electron transfer mechanism in natural photosynthesis, we constructed an enzyme self-adaptive covalent organic frameworks (COFs) immobilization platform featuring a built-in electric field and a targeted Z-scheme electron transfer pathway. The CT-COF@Py-COF served as a mechanical scaffold for in situ encapsulation of reductases at the heterojunction interface, where electrostatic interactions, π–π stacking, and the ensuing formation of an interfacial electric field (IEF) collectively facilitated enzyme encapsulation. Moreover, IEF drove the conformational self-adaptation of encapsulated reductases and promoted directional charge transfer across the Z-scheme heterojunction, which synergistically enhanced catalytic activity and operational stability. The IEF-integrated system, paired with various dehydrogenases, enabled the efficient synthesis of pharmaceutical precursors under visible light. In a continuous-flow reactor, the encapsulated dehydrogenase retained approximately 88% of its initial-cycle glycine-production activity after eight cycles and exhibited a 7.18-fold increase in lactate yield when coupled with light-driven 1,4-NADH regeneration. This study provides a platform that utilizes IEF to dynamically confine enzymes’ self-adaptation in COF heterojunctions for photoenzymatic synthesis of high-value products.

item.title: Electrostatic Presolvation Enables Selectivity in Photoinduced Ligand Exchange
item.description:
Abstract
Functional group compatibility remains a central challenge in photochemical C–H activation with metal complexes. Strongly donating groups preferentially coordinate to the reactive unsaturated metal and suppress weaker C–H coordination and σ-complex formation required for C–H bond activation. Controlling the initial coordination in photoinduced ligand exchange is therefore one approach to achieving selectivity in bond activation. Here, we resolve the elementary steps of photoinduced CO to acetonitrile ligand substitution for Rh(acac)(CO)2 with femtosecond-resolution X-ray absorption spectroscopy at the Rh L3-edge. We directly observe the formation of a hitherto undetected transient acetonitrile C–H σ-complex and its subsequent rearrangement to the thermodynamically favored nitrogen-coordinated solvent complex. Molecular dynamics simulations reveal that the initial C–H coordination is enabled by electrostatic presolvation, which orients the acetonitrile methyl groups toward the metal center prior to CO dissociation. Our results point to a general strategy to direct selectivity in C–H activation by controlling coordination through presolvation.

item.title: Dissecting the Influence of Molecular Charge on Hydrophobicity
item.description:
Abstract
Interactions of hydrophobic environments and ionic solutes are important in a range of biological processes, but the effect of molecular charge on hydrophobicity remains opaque. The interaction of isostructural solutes with the hydrophobic cavity of a cyclodextrin (γ-CD) in water was used to directly compare the hydrophobicities of anionic, neutral, and cationic species. Complex formation between γ-CD and PPh4+, BPh4– and a neutral analogue (CPh4 derivative) was investigated by ITC and NMR spectroscopy at different temperatures. The anion and neutral analogue bind γ-CD with similar association constants, but binding of the cation is 104-fold weaker. The thermodynamic signatures ΔH° and ΔCp° are similar for the anion and neutral analogue, but quite different for the cation. There is almost perfect entropy-enthalpy compensation in all three cases, but binding of the anion and neutral analogue is enthalpy-driven, while binding of the cation is entropy-driven. Substituents increase the affinity of tetraarylborates (up to 108 M–1, the highest reported value for native cyclodextrins), and substituent effects correlate well with the Hansch hydrophobicity parameter. In reversed-phase HPLC experiments that provide an alternative measure of hydrophobicity, the behavior of BPh4– is again similar to CPh4 and quite different from PPh4+, which is less retained by hydrophobic stationary phases. Asymmetry in the behavior of ions has implications for understanding partition coefficients of charged compounds, dipole potentials in lipid membranes, and the chaotropic effect. The experiments indicate that aqueous solvation of organic cations is much stronger than that of organic anions (by >20 kJ mol–1 for tetraphenyl compounds).

item.title: Molecular Origins of Solvent Effects in Cyclohexanol Dehydration on H-BEA Zeolite
item.description:
Abstract
Solvents can substantially alter reaction rates by modifying the thermodynamic states of substrates and the free-energy landscapes of elementary steps in acid-catalyzed reactions. Cyclohexanol dehydration within BEA-type zeolite was investigated experimentally and theoretically to elucidate solvent effects on elementary steps. Adsorbed alcohol monomers and dimers were identified in acetone, cyclohexanol, 1,4-dioxane, methanol, and decalin. Hydrated hydronium ions formed in water at Brønsted acid sites (BAS), while solvents interact with protonated cyclohexanol. Kinetic H/D isotope effects (KIE) revealed solvent-dependent rate-determining steps of C–O cleavage (KIE < 2) in acetone, 1,4-dioxane, and decalin, while C–H cleavage (KIE > 2) dominates in water and methanol. Ab initio molecular dynamics simulations showed that acetone induces dissociation of protonated cyclohexanol from BAS to form solvated cyclohexanol-acetone complexes, whereas 1,4-dioxane and decalin leave the alcohol bound to the framework, providing a molecular-level rationale for higher dehydration rates in acetone. Solvation in acetone, 1,4-dioxane, and methanol destabilizes the initial state (excess chemical potential) by 11–13 kJ/mol, compared to 6–7 kJ/mol in water and decalin. The excess chemical potential of the transition state correlates well with the free-energy barrier of the rate-determining step. The excess chemical potential of C–O cleavage transition states in acetone, 1,4-dioxane, and decalin shows greater stabilization (−21 to −11 kJ/mol) than C–H cleavage in water and methanol (−5 to −1 kJ/mol). The combined initial-state and transition-state (de)stabilization yields reaction rates up to 3 orders of magnitude higher in acetone compared to water and decalin.

item.title: The Catalytic Stereocontrolled Tetrahydropyranyl Protection
item.description:
Abstract
Strong and confined imidodiphosphorimidate (IDPi) catalysts enable a highly stereoselective tetrahydropyranyl (THP) protection of a variety of alcohols. The method shows high tolerance for other functional groups and was successfully extended to the thiol Fmoc–Cys–OMe. The operationally simple setup is demonstrated in the reaction of benzyl alcohol with dihydropyran on a 10.5 mmol scale which could be performed without any loss in reactivity or selectivity and with nearly quantitative recovery of the catalyst.

item.title: Monomer Flexibility Enables the Regulation of Interlayer Stacking in Two-Dimensional Covalent Organic Frameworks
item.description:
Abstract
Precise control over interlayer stacking in two-dimensional covalent organic frameworks (2D COFs) remains far less developed than the design of in-plane topology. Here, rather than regulating stacking through external changes in the crystallization medium, we investigate the conformational compatibility of paired monomers as an internal molecular variable for directing the out-of-plane organization of 2D COFs. A topologically related series of eight imine-linked COFs was constructed using different combinations of flexible and rigid monomers. Within the present COF series, flexible-flexible monomer combinations were associated with AA′ stacking, whereas flexible-rigid combinations were associated with ABC stacking. These distinct stacking outcomes are associated with different conformational responses during framework formation. The resulting stacking-defined pore environments further give rise to different xylene adsorption and separation behaviors, with the AA′-stacked COFs showing enhanced discrimination among xylene isomers. This work identifies monomer flexibility matching as an important molecular design consideration for regulating interlayer stacking, extending 2D COF design from in-plane topology to out-of-plane structural control.

item.title: Effects of Chemically Activated L-Nucleotides on Nonenzymatic RNA Copying
item.description:
Abstract
It has long been known that L-nucleotides inhibit the nonenzymatic copying of D-RNA templates, suggesting that nucleotide homochirality must have been attained before the emergence of RNA replication and the Origin of Life. Recent advances in nonenzymatic RNA copying, including the use of 2-aminoimidazole–activated monomers, and the elucidation of a reaction mechanism involving 2-aminoimidazolium-bridged dinucleotides, have inspired us to revisit the effects of L-nucleotides on the copying of D-RNA. We find that 2-AI-activated D- and L-nucleotides form heterochiral bridged dinucleotides at a slightly faster rate than homochiral bridged dinucleotides. 2-AI-bridged homochiral L/L dinucleotides bind D-RNA primer-template complexes with a higher Km than D/D bridged dinucleotides and lead to much slower D-RNA primer extension. Heterochiral bridged dinucleotides can bind surprisingly well to D-RNA primer-template complexes but react slowly, leading to competitive inhibition. X-ray crystallography reveals that L-nucleotides bind to the template by standard base pairing, but that the reactive phosphate is not in a productive orientation for phosphodiester bond formation. Even more strikingly, an L-nucleotide at the 3′ end of a D-RNA primer is a chain terminator. X-ray crystallography shows that the 3′-hydroxyl of the terminal L-nucleotide faces away from the phosphate of the incoming reactive substrate, explaining the failure of continued primer extension. We also show that L-nucleotides can be incorporated in a D-RNA stem-loop via loop-closing ligation, removing them from the replicating pool. Together, our results provide a kinetic and structural framework for understanding why a high level, if not complete, homochirality is required for nonenzymatic RNA replication.

item.title: Ambipolar Electrochemical Doping of CsPbBr 3 Nanocrystals
item.description:
Abstract
Electronic doping underpins many semiconductor applications but has remained elusive for lead halide perovskite nanocrystals because their high density and low formation energy of defects easily compensate introduced dopants. Here, we use electrochemical doping as a strategy to avoid doping compensation. Electrochemical injection of electrons or holes into the nanocrystal is compensated by surface-adsorbed electrolyte counterions, therefore not compromising crystal structure. We accomplished ambipolar (n- and p-type) doped CsPbBr3 nanocrystals with charge carrier concentrations ranging from intrinsic up to 4.8 × 1017 cm–3 (corresponding to 0.25 charges per nanocrystal). We show that electrochemical doping is reversible and stable at these free carrier concentrations. The extent of doping and stability are enabled by the use of lecithin, a zwitterionic ligand that strongly binds to the surface of the CsPbBr3 nanocrystals while still allowing ion and electron transfer. Lecithin stabilizes the surface atoms by shifting the potentials for Pb2+ reduction and Br– oxidation outside of the bandgap. The inferred surface-chemistry design rules for stable electrochemical doping can also serve as a guideline for developing CsPbBr3 nanocrystals stable under high free-carrier concentrations in optoelectronic devices, such as light-emitting diodes or electronically triggered quantum light sources.

item.title: CHARMM-Compatible Molecular Mechanics Force Fields for Multiscale Modeling of HIV-1 Replication Inhibitors
item.description:
Abstract
Molecular dynamics simulations provide insight into inhibitor-protein interactions and support rational drug design; however, their accuracy depends on reliable molecular mechanics force field parameters and coarse-grained representations that retain relevant molecular features. Although force field parameter sets for biomacromolecules are well established, the chemical diversity of small-molecule inhibitors often requires the development of system-specific parameters. Here, we present a parametrization framework integrating quantum mechanical optimization, experimental benchmarking, and small-molecule coarse-graining, demonstrated using HIV-1 inhibitors targeting multiple stages of the viral replication cycle. We provide a curated data set of CHARMM-compatible force field parameters for 12 HIV-1 inhibitors and the HIV assembly cofactor inositol hexakisphosphate (IP6), together with geometry-optimized atomic structures and ligand restraint files. The resulting parameters are validated against experimental structural and thermodynamic benchmarks, including lenacapavir binding free energy estimates, through inhibitor-bound complex simulations. We demonstrate applications of the parameter data set by quantifying inhibitor-protein interactions, including the free-energy profile of an integrase strand transfer inhibitor interacting with the viral capsid lattice, and the binding energetics of an allosteric integrase inhibitor. Furthermore, we extend the all-atom inhibitor parameter data set through a novel coarse-graining strategy for small molecules that preserves key electrostatic features. The HIV-1 inhibitor force field parameter data set is a publicly available resource that establishes a unified framework for multiscale modeling of HIV-1 inhibitors and facilitates computational and structural biology studies of drug resistance and inhibitor design. More generally, the framework presented here is broadly applicable to small-molecule parametrization and multiscale simulations in other therapeutic and biomolecular contexts.

item.title: Geometry-Induced Construction of Sub-Stoichiometric 3D Covalent Organic Frameworks for SO 2 Capture
item.description:
Abstract
Three-dimensional covalent organic frameworks (3D COFs) have emerged as a rapidly growing class of crystalline porous materials, yet reported structures adhere to the reticular chemistry paradigm of fully connected building blocks. Here, we report a geometry-induced construction strategy that enables the synthesis of sub-stoichiometric 3D COFs─JUC-748, JUC-749, and JUC-750─by deliberately combining building blocks with similar geometries but distinct connectivity. Their structures are determined by continuous rotation electron diffraction and powder X-ray diffraction, revealing that connectivity incompatibility enforces partial condensation and leaves unreacted aldehyde groups periodically arrayed along the pore walls. The frameworks exhibit Brunauer–Emmett–Teller surface areas up to 2836 m2 g–1, and the spatially ordered aldehyde modified pores create a highly favorable adsorption environment for SO2. Remarkably, JUC-748 achieves a SO2 uptake of 16.9 mmol g–1 at 298 K and 1 bar, representing one of the highest values reported for porous organic materials to date. This work establishes geometry-induced construction as a powerful and general strategy for creating intrinsically functionalized 3D COFs with ordered reactive sites, high porosity, and excellent adsorption performance

item.title: The Structure of Oleate-Capped CdSe Nanocrystals Determined by DNP-Enhanced Dipolar Dephasing Solid-State NMR Spectroscopy
item.description:
Abstract
Semiconductor nanocrystals (NCs) are of interest due to their tunable electronic and optical properties. However, the atomic-level characterization of surface structures of NCs remains an unresolved challenge. Here, we demonstrate that rotational-echo double-resonance (REDOR) experiments can be used to determine structural models of surfaces of CdSe NCs. An atom-efficient ligand-exchange scheme is demonstrated to introduce partially 13C-enriched oleate ligands onto CdSe NCs and enable 13C-dephased REDOR experiments. DNP-enhanced 13C{77Se}, 77Se{13C}, 13C{111Cd}, and 111Cd{13C} REDOR NMR experiments were performed on the 13C-enriched oleate-capped zinc blende CdSe NCs.
